title: Wasserstein Autonomy: Optimal Transport of Harness States
text:
So here’s a question that keeps coming up in conversations about coding agents: how much actual engineering work sits between a fully scaffolded harness and one that runs with barely any human in the loop? We recast this question as a Kantorovich optimal-transport (OT) problem between two probability measures on a partially ordered constraint lattice, and out of that framing falls a provable lower bound—the Wasserstein-2 distance (W₂)—on the irreducible cost of getting to autonomy. The dual formulation gives you a certifiable refactoring schedule, and the whole thing slots neatly into the entropy, free-energy, and percolation threads we’ve been pulling through this series.

What you will get from this post

A formal W₂ lower bound on the refactoring cost between any two harness configurations.
A dual-potential certificate you can actually drop into a CI pipeline and have it audited.
A seven-step algorithm that turns the bound into an ordered, dependency-respecting work schedule.
Explicit connections to the rate-distortion, free-energy, and percolation results elsewhere in this series.


Prerequisites. Fair warning: this post assumes you’re comfortable with basic measure theory, the Kantorovich formulation of OT, and enough lattice theory to follow the partial-order notation. If OT is new to you, Villani (2009), Chapters 1–2, is the classic entry point, or the more accessible survey in Peyré & Cuturi (2019), Chapter 1, will get you there. For the broader autonomy-spectrum model we’re building on, see The Autonomy Imperative.

title: Wasserstein Autonomy: Optimal Transport of Harness States
text:
1. Why Transport, Not Enumeration
“How far is my harness from full autonomy?” Sounds like a simple question, right? The naive move is to enumerate: list the constraints you need to pull, the invariants you need to loosen, the feedback loops you need to rewire, and then sum up the person-hours. And sure, you can do that. But it’s fragile. The order in which you relax things matters—some relaxations are only possible after others are in place. And the geometry of the constraint space (its partial order, its symmetries, its critical thresholds) sets a cost floor that no clever scheduling can get below.
Optimal transport gives us exactly the right language for this. Instead of asking “which constraints do I remove?”, the question becomes “what’s the minimum work to deform the probability measure describing my current harness into the one describing the target autonomous state?” The W₂ distance between those two measures is that minimum work. Concretely, it’s the cost of moving mass—engineering attention, test coverage, guardrail density—from wherever the scaffolded regime puts it to wherever the autonomous regime needs it, subject to the geometric constraints of the lattice.
And this isn’t just a pretty reframing. It buys you three things: (i) a lower bound that doesn’t care what schedule you pick, (ii) a dual certificate you can verify without enumerating the full coupling, and (iii) a natural bridge to the rate-distortion floor in The Autonomy Channel and the free-energy bound in Free Energy Bounds.

title: Wasserstein Autonomy: Optimal Transport of Harness States
section: 2. The Constraint Lattice and Its Measures
text:
2. The Constraint Lattice and Its Measures

2.1 The Lattice \(\mathcal{L}\)
A harness configuration is modelled as an element \(a \in \mathcal{L}\) of a finite distributive lattice \((\mathcal{L}, \preceq)\). The atoms are individual constraints—input-validation rules, output-checklist gates, sandbox isolation levels, human-approval checkpoints, that sort of thing. The order \(\preceq\) encodes weakening: \(a \preceq b\) means configuration \(b\) has relaxed (or removed) at least the constraints present in \(a\). Top element \(\top\) is the fully scaffolded harness; bottom element \(\bot\) is maximal autonomy (nothing left beyond the irreducible safety invariants we identified in Cohomological Obstructions).
The distance between two configurations is defined via an effort function:
\[d(a, b) \;=\; \text{effort}(a \to b),\]
where \(\text{effort}(a \to b)\) is the engineering cost (person-hours, CI-cycle-equivalents, whatever normalised unit you like) of going from configuration \(a\) to \(b\) along the shortest dependency-respecting path in \(\mathcal{L}\).
Estimating the effort function. This is the single most important empirical input to the whole framework, and honestly, it deserves way more attention than a one-line definition gets. In practice, you’ll calibrate \(\text{effort}(a \to b)\) from a few sources:

CI/CD telemetry. Wall-clock time and retry counts for the sequence of test-suite changes needed to pass under relaxed constraints.
Pull-request review data. Median review time and revision cycles for PRs that touch the same guardrail files.
Historical refactoring logs. If your team has already walked part of the lattice, the realised effort for each transition \((a, b)\) is a direct sample.
Expert elicitation. For transitions nobody’s traversed yet, structured Delphi estimates (anchored on the ones you have traversed) give you a defensible prior.

The key requirement is that \(d\) satisfy the triangle inequality on \(\mathcal{L}\). It need not be symmetric if adding constraints costs differently than removing them, but for the W₂ formulation we assume symmetry (or restrict to the directed setting). A companion post will develop a proper statistical estimator for \(\text{effort}\) from heterogeneous telemetry; for now, treat it as given.


2.2 Probability Measures on \(\mathcal{L}\)
Here’s the point that trips people up: a harness state isn’t a single lattice element. In production, you’re running across multiple codebases, feature branches, deployment environments—so the state is really a distribution over lattice elements. Formally, a harness state is a probability measure \(\mu \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{L})\) (for finite \(\mathcal{L}\), just a probability vector). The scaffolded state \(\mu_S\) concentrates mass near \(\top\); the autonomous target \(\mu_A\) concentrates near \(\bot\).

title: Wasserstein Autonomy: Optimal Transport of Harness States
text:
3. The Worked Example

Concrete anchor. Let’s make this tangible. Picture a small harness with four constraints: input validation (IV), output checklist (OC), sandbox isolation (SI), and human approval (HA). The lattice has \(2^4 = 16\) elements (all subsets of active constraints). The scaffolded state \(\mu_S\) puts 80% mass on the full set \(\{IV, OC, SI, HA\}\) and 20% on \(\{IV, SI, HA\}\). The autonomous target \(\mu_A\) puts 70% mass on \(\{IV\}\) and 30% on \(\{IV, SI\}\).
The effort function, calibrated from (say) a year of CI logs, looks like this: removing HA costs 40 h; removing OC costs 25 h; removing SI costs 60 h (because it requires re-architecting the sandbox boundary); adding any constraint back costs 10 h per constraint. The W₂ distance between \(\mu_S\) and \(\mu_A\) comes out of solving the linear programme over the \(16 \times 16\) coupling matrix. The optimal coupling assigns the 70% mass at \(\{IV, OC, SI, HA\}\) to \(\{IV\}\) at cost \(d^2 = (40+25+60)^2 = 18225\), and the 30% mass at \(\{IV, SI, HA\}\) to \(\{IV, SI\}\) at cost \(d^2 = 40^2 = 1600\). The W₂ value is \(\sqrt{0.7 \cdot 18225 + 0.3 \cdot 1600} \approx 112.4\) (in \(\sqrt{\text{h}^2}\) units).
Interpretation. No matter how cleverly you sequence the refactoring, the total effort can’t fall below \(\approx 112.4^2 \approx 12{,}630\) h² (or \(\approx 112.4\) h in the linearised reading). That’s the irreducible cost.

What I like about this example is the key property it exposes: the W₂ bound is schedule-independent. Whether the team pulls HA first, or OC first, or parallelises the SI re-architecture alongside the HA removal—the total effort can’t dip below the bound. Period.

title: Wasserstein Autonomy: Optimal Transport of Harness States
text:
4. The Dual Formulation

4.1 Primal and Dual
The primal Wasserstein-2 problem is
\[W_2^2(\mu, \nu) \;=\; \inf_{\gamma \in \Pi(\mu,\nu)} \int_{\mathcal{L} \times \mathcal{L}} d(a,b)^2 \, d\gamma(a,b),\]
where \(\Pi(\mu,\nu)\) is the set of all couplings (joint distributions with marginals \(\mu\) and \(\nu\)).
By the Kantorovich dual, this equals
\[\boxed{\;W_2^2(\mu, \nu) \;=\; \sup_{\varphi, \psi} \;\left\{ \int \varphi \, d\mu \;+\; \int \psi \, d\nu \;\;\middle|\;\; \varphi(a) + \psi(b) \;\leq\; d(a,b)^2 \;\;\forall\, a,b \in \mathcal{L} \right\}.\;}\]
Let me translate that into plain English: the squared W₂ distance equals the best you can do by assigning a “price” \(\varphi(a)\) to every source configuration and a “value” \(\psi(b)\) to every target, subject to the single rule that no pair’s combined price-and-value may exceed the squared transport cost between them.
For finite \(\mathcal{L}\), the dual is a linear programme with \(2|\mathcal{L}|\) variables and \(|\mathcal{L}|^2\) inequality constraints. Here’s where it gets practically useful: a feasible dual pair \((\varphi, \psi)\) is a certificate. If someone on the team proposes a refactoring schedule with total cost \(C\), and \(\int \varphi\, d\mu + \int \psi\, d\nu > C\), then that schedule is provably suboptimal. You can check this in CI. No hand-waving required.


4.2 Existence and Uniqueness
For the discrete setting (finite \(\mathcal{L}\)), the optimal coupling always exists—the feasible set \(\Pi(\mu,\nu)\) is compact and the objective is linear, so you’re done. Uniqueness is a bit more delicate: it holds whenever the cost matrix \((d(a_i, b_j)^2)_{ij}\) is non-degenerate in the sense that no two distinct pairs \((a_i, b_j) \neq (a_k, \ell)\) share the same cost value (Murota, 2003, Ch. 5). When the cost matrix has ties, the optimal coupling is unique up to the face of the coupling polytope that’s degenerate, and any element of that face works. In practice, the strict lattice ordering of \(\mathcal{L}\) and the monotonicity of \(\text{effort}\) keep things non-degenerate for all but pathological effort assignments.

title: Wasserstein Autonomy: Optimal Transport of Harness States
section: 5. The Optimal Coupling as a Refactoring Schedule
text:
5. The Optimal Coupling as a Refactoring Schedule
Now, the optimal coupling \(\gamma^*\) isn’t just some abstract probability distribution sitting in a vector space. Because \(\mathcal{L}\) is a poset, the support of \(\gamma^*\)—the set of pairs \((a, b)\) with \(\gamma^*(a, b) > 0\)—induces a partial order on the refactoring steps. Concretely: if \(\gamma^*\) assigns mass to \((a_1, b_1)\) and \((a_2, b_2)\) with \(a_1 \preceq a_2\) but \(b_1 \not\preceq b_2\), then the transition for \((a_1, b_1)\) must be finished before \((a_2, b_2)\) can start. Topologically sort that partial order, and you’ve got a concrete, dependency-respecting schedule.

The schedule is order-preserving: it never asks you to remove a constraint before its prerequisites are in place. That’s a direct consequence of the lattice structure and the monotonicity of the cost. It means the W₂ schedule is always a valid engineering plan—whereas an arbitrary enumeration might happily propose pulling the sandbox before the approval gate that depends on it. (I’ve seen that happen in planning documents. Don’t.)

title: Wasserstein Autonomy: Optimal Transport of Harness States
text:
6. Entropy and the Transport Cost
The coupling \(\gamma\) is a joint distribution, so it carries a Shannon entropy \(H(\gamma) = -\sum_{a,b} \gamma(a,b) \log \gamma(a,b)\). A deterministic coupling (a bijection between support points of \(\mu\) and \(\nu\)) has \(H(\gamma) = 0\); a maximally mixed coupling hits \(H(\gamma) = \log(|\mathcal{L}|)\).
What does the entropy of the optimal coupling actually tell you? It measures the intrinsic ambiguity in the refactoring schedule. If \(H(\gamma^*) > 0\), there are multiple ways to route the mass and the team has genuine scheduling freedom. If \(H(\gamma^*) = 0\), the schedule is rigid—every unit of mass must travel along a single, uniquely determined path. In the worked example from §3, \(H(\gamma^*) = 0\) because the support has exactly two points and the masses match one-to-one.
Entropy also feeds into the rate-distortion connection. As we showed in The Autonomy Channel, the minimum “description length” of a harness configuration at distortion level \(D\) is governed by \(R(D)\), and the W₂ cost provides a geometric realisation of that distortion.

title: Wasserstein Autonomy: Optimal Transport of Harness States
text:
7. Free-Energy Connection
The free-energy functional we introduced in Free Energy Bounds is
\[F(\mu) \;=\; \int \Phi(a) \, d\mu(a) \;+\; T \, H(\mu),\]
where \(\Phi: \mathcal{L} \to \mathbb{R}\) is the constraint-potential (the “energy” of a configuration, increasing with the number of active constraints), \(T > 0\) is a temperature parameter (think: engineering slack), and \(H(\mu)\) is the entropy of the harness state.
Now, assume the interpolation \(\mu_t\) between \(\mu_S\) and \(\mu_A\) follows the gradient flow of \(F\) (i.e., \(\partial_t \mu_t = -\nabla_{\mu} F(\mu_t)\) in the Wasserstein tangent space). The Benamou–Brenier kinetic-energy identity then gives
\[W_2^2(\mu_S, \mu_A) \;=\; \inf_{\mu_t} \int_0^1 \int_{\mathcal{L}} \frac{|\nabla \varphi_t(a)|^2}{2} \, d\mu_t(a) \, dt.\]
Under that same gradient-flow assumption, the chain rule yields
\[\frac{d}{dt} F(\mu_t) \;=\; -\int_{\mathcal{L}} \frac{|\nabla \varphi_t(a)|^2}{2} \, d\mu_t(a),\]
so integrating from \(t=0\) to \(t=1\):
\[\boxed{\;W_2^2(\mu_S, \mu_A) \;=\; F(\mu_S) - F(\mu_A).\;}\]
In words: the squared transport cost equals the drop in free energy between the scaffolded and autonomous states. This isn’t a coincidence—it’s the Wasserstein analogue of the thermodynamic fact that work equals the change in free energy along a reversible path.
The practical upshot: the per-step KL budget from Free Energy Bounds reads as a local bound on the instantaneous transport speed \(|\nabla \varphi_t|^2 / 2\), while the W₂ bound is the global integral of that speed over the full transition. One is the speedometer; the other is the odometer.

title: Wasserstein Autonomy: Optimal Transport of Harness States
section: 8. Percolation Threshold and the W₂ Bound
text:
8. Percolation Threshold and the W₂ Bound
In Percolation of Autonomy, we model the constraint lattice as a site-percolation process: each constraint is “active” (scaffolded) with probability \(p\), and autonomy emerges when the active-constraint cluster percolates. The critical threshold \(p_c\) is where the expected cluster size diverges.
The W₂ bound interacts with this in a sharp way. Define the autonomy deficit at threshold as
\[\Delta W_2^2 \;=\; W_2^2(\mu_S, \mu_A) \Big|_{p = p_c} \;-\; W_2^2(\mu_S, \mu_A) \Big|_{p \to 0}.\]
Near \(p_c\), the cluster size scales as \(\langle s \rangle \sim |p - p_c|^{-\nu}\) (with \(\nu \approx 4/3\) in 2D, \(\nu \approx 0.876\) in 3D; Stauffer & Aharony, 1994). The W₂ cost inherits this divergence: as \(p \to p_c^-\), the optimal coupling must route mass through increasingly large intermediate clusters, and \(W_2^2\) blows up as \(|p_c - p|^{-2\nu}\).
What this means in practice is that the last increment of autonomy—the final relaxation of the last percolating constraint cluster—is disproportionately expensive. The W₂ bound makes that quantitative. You should expect a power-law blow-up in effort as the harness approaches the critical threshold, and you should plan buffer capacity accordingly. The RG-flow cascade algorithm in Coarse-Graining Autonomy gives you a practical method for identifying which constraints belong to the percolating cluster and scheduling their relaxation before you hit the critical window.

title: Wasserstein Autonomy: Optimal Transport of Harness States
text:
9. Practical Algorithm
Here’s the seven-step pipeline that converts the W₂ bound into an actionable refactoring plan. A reference implementation in Python, built on the POT library (Peyré & Cuturi, 2019) with a custom lattice-distance kernel, lives at the companion repository (placeholder; see project page for the live link).

Enumerate the lattice. List all constraint configurations \(a_1, \ldots, a_N\) and the partial order \(\preceq\). (For \(k\) independent constraints, \(N = 2^k\); for correlated constraints, \(N\) is smaller.)
Calibrate the effort function. Populate the \(N \times N\) cost matrix \(d(a_i, a_j)\) from CI telemetry, PR review data, and expert estimates (§2.1).
Specify the target measure. Define \(\mu_A\) by listing the desired constraint configurations and their target probabilities across the deployment fleet.
Solve the dual LP. Run a linear programme (e.g., scipy.optimize.linprog or a commercial solver) to get the optimal potentials \((\varphi^*, \psi^*)\). The objective value is \(W_2^2\).
Extract the coupling. Recover \(\gamma^*\) from the complementary-slackness conditions: \(\gamma^*(a,b) > 0\) only where \(\varphi^*(a) + \psi^*(b) = d(a,b)^2\).
Topologically sort the support. Build the DAG from the support of \(\gamma^*\) and produce the ordered refactoring schedule (§5).
Emit the certificate. Write \((\varphi^*, \psi^*)\) to a machine-readable file. Downstream CI checks can then verify that any proposed schedule with cost \(C\) satisfies \(C \geq \int \varphi^*\, d\mu_S + \int \psi^*\, d\mu_A\).

The whole pipeline runs in \(O(N^3)\) time for the LP (dominated by the \(N^2\) constraint matrix), which is tractable up to \(N \leq 10^4\)—comfortably beyond the \(2^{20} \approx 10^6\) configurations of a 20-constraint harness.

title: Wasserstein Autonomy: Optimal Transport of Harness States
text:
10. Discussion and Open Questions
Relation to the geodesic framework. The W₂ geodesic between \(\mu_S\) and \(\mu_A\) is the unique (up to the non-degeneracy condition) constant-speed path in \(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{L})\) that minimises kinetic energy. This is the same geodesic we identified in Autonomy as Geodesic, where the Riemannian metric on \(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{L})\) is induced by the lattice distance \(d\). What this post adds is the dual certificate and the percolation sensitivity layered on top of that geometric picture.
Relation to functorial structure. You can view the optimal coupling \(\gamma^*\) as a natural transformation between the “scaffolded” and “autonomous” functors on the constraint category, in the sense we developed in Functorial Autonomy. The W₂ bound then becomes a lower bound on the “distance” between natural transformations, and the dual potentials are component-wise witnesses of the naturality square. (I know, I know—category theory. But it earns its keep here.)
Multi-agent case. When the harness has to coordinate \(n > 2\) concurrent agent instances (say, a coder, a reviewer, and a security auditor), the single coupling \(\gamma\) is replaced by a joint distribution on \(\mathcal{L}^n\) with prescribed marginals. The dual becomes a system of \(n\) coupled potentials \((\varphi_1, \ldots, \varphi_n)\) with \(n(n-1)/2\) cross-constraints. The W₂ bound generalises to the multi-marginal Wasserstein distance, and the dual LP has \(n \cdot N\) variables. The percolation analysis extends naturally: the critical threshold now governs the simultaneous percolation of \(n\) interdependent constraint clusters. Full treatment deferred to a subsequent post—this one’s already long enough.
Gauge invariance. As we showed in Gauge Symmetry and the Invariant Core, many distinct lattice elements are gauge-equivalent: they differ only in the labelling of constraints, not in their structural role. The W₂ distance is gauge-invariant (it depends only on the orbit of \(\mu\) under the gauge group), so the bound is well-defined on the quotient space \(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{L}) / \mathcal{G}\). This reduces the effective dimension of the LP and kills the spurious cost differences that creep in from arbitrary constraint naming.
Cohomological obstructions. Not every target \(\mu_A\) is reachable by any finite sequence of constraint relaxations. As proved in Cohomological Obstructions, non-trivial elements of \(H^1(\mathcal{L}; \mathbb{Z})\) obstruct the existence of a global section of the constraint-bundle, meaning no coupling \(\gamma\) exists for certain target measures. The W₂ problem is then infeasible, and the dual LP flags this via unboundedness of the dual objective. Practical advice: run the feasibility check (Step 4) before you invest in the full schedule. Saves you a week of work.
If you are looking for adjacent topics: this post sits at the intersection of LLM agent evaluation methodology, coding-agent guardrail design, refactoring cost estimation, and quantitative software-architecture trade-offs. The spectral-conditioning result in The Spectral Gap of Autonomy gives a complementary convergence-speed bound, while the dialectical framing in Scaffolding to Sovereignty tackles the philosophical question of whether scaffolding is a prerequisite or a hindrance.

title: Wasserstein Autonomy: Optimal Transport of Harness States
text:
11. Conclusion
So. We’ve recast the scaffold-to-autonomy transition as a Kantorovich optimal-transport problem on a constraint lattice. The W₂ distance between the scaffolded and autonomous harness states gives you a schedule-independent lower bound on refactoring effort. The dual potentials give you a CI-auditable certificate. And the optimal coupling, read against the lattice order, produces a concrete, dependency-respecting work schedule. The bound sharpens with the entropy of the coupling, aligns with the free-energy drop along the autonomy geodesic, and diverges at the percolation threshold—quantifying the disproportionate cost of that final increment of autonomy.
The practical message, if you take nothing else from this post: before your team starts ripping out guardrails, compute the W₂ bound. It tells you, in a single number, how much effort is irreducibly required. And the dual certificate tells you, in a single file, whether any proposed schedule can beat it.
The distance between a scaffolded harness and an autonomous one is not a matter of opinion, priority, or political negotiation. It is a number, and it is provably the smallest one that will do.

title: Autonomy as Geodesic: Information Geometry of Harness Design
text:
We recast the space of all parametrically defined coding-agent harness configurations as a statistical manifold equipped with the Fisher information metric. Every shift in autonomy level becomes a geodesic trajectory whose length, curvature, and parallel transport carry precise engineering meaning. The payoff? A differential-geometric calculus in which “how hard is it to make a harness more autonomous?” stops being an ad-hoc design heuristic and becomes a computable quantity.


Full abstract (paper-style)

Let \(\mathcal{H}\) denote the set of all parametrically specified harnesses for a coding agent, and let \(\theta \in \Theta \subset \mathbb{R}^n\) be the vector of design parameters (constraint densities, permission scopes, verification gates, feedback-loop gains, etc.). For each \(\theta\), the agent’s behavior is summarized by a conditional distribution \(p_\theta(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{x})\) over task outcomes. Equipping \(\Theta\) with the Fisher information metric \(g_{ij}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_\theta[\partial_i \log p_\theta \;\partial_j \log p_\theta]\) turns \((\Theta, g)\) into a Riemannian manifold \(\mathcal{M}\). We show that (i) optimal autonomy transitions are geodesics; (ii) the sectional curvature at \(\theta\) quantifies the sensitivity of that transition to the order in which sub-constraints are relaxed; (iii) parallel transport along a geodesic defines a canonical way to carry constraint semantics from a lower-autonomy regime to a higher one without “twist.” We derive a design calculus: given a target autonomy level, the engineer computes the geodesic, reads off its length (effort), curvature (fragility), and holonomy (semantic drift), and thereby obtains a principled, quantitative answer to the central question of harness design.

title: Autonomy as Geodesic: Information Geometry of Harness Design
text:
Key Takeaways

Autonomy transitions are paths, not jumps. The geometric distance between two harness configurations (measured by the Fisher information metric) is the true cost of reconfiguration—not the number of parameters you happen to change.
Curvature is fragility. High sectional curvature near a configuration means the order in which you relax constraints actually matters; low curvature means the transition is robust to sequencing.
Parallel transport is semantic preservation. Carrying a constraint’s meaning along a geodesic without holonomy is just the math way of saying “the agent still understands what ‘safe’ means” at the new autonomy level.
A 2-D worked example (Gaussian-parameter manifold) shows how to compute the geodesic, the curvature, and the effort integral by hand.
The workflow is concrete: estimate the Fisher metric on your task suite, solve the geodesic ODE, read off length and curvature, and iterate.

title: Autonomy as Geodesic: Information Geometry of Harness Design
text:
1. The Manifold of Harness Configurations
So what is a coding-agent harness, really? It’s the parametric scaffold that governs what an LLM-based agent is allowed to perceive, decide, and execute across the software development lifecycle. Concretely, a harness is a tuple \(\mathbf{h} = (\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{P}, \mathcal{V}, \mathcal{F})\) comprising a set of scope rules \(\mathcal{S}\), a permission matrix \(\mathcal{P}\), a verification gate \(\mathcal{V}\), and a feedback controller \(\mathcal{F}\). Each component gets parameterized by a finite vector, and you collect the whole thing into a single parameter vector \(\theta \in \Theta \subset \mathbb{R}^n\).
For a given \(\theta\), the agent’s observable behavior on a task distribution \(\mathcal{D}\) is captured by a conditional outcome distribution \(p_\theta(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{x})\), where \(\mathbf{x}\) is the task specification and \(\mathbf{y}\) is the vector of deliverable properties (correctness, security, style compliance, and so on). The mapping \(\theta \mapsto p_\theta\) is, in the classical sense (Amari & Nagaoka, 2000), a statistical model.
Now here’s where it gets geometric. The set of all such configurations \(\Theta\)—modulo reparameterization invariance—forms a smooth manifold \(\mathcal{M}\). It’s smooth wherever the parameterization is regular, meaning the Fisher information matrix stays positive-definite. Its topology inherits from the ambient parameter space, modulo the equivalence class of reparameterizations that leave the induced distribution family unchanged. This resonates with the gauge-symmetry reduction I explored in Gauge Symmetry and the Invariant Core of Harness Autonomy, where combinatorially distinct harnesses collapse into a finite set of inequivalent autonomy structures.
Engineering reading. You don’t need to know differential geometry to use this framework. What matters is this: your harness is a point on a curved surface, and moving it costs something. The cost isn’t the number of toggles you flip; it’s the geometric distance you traverse.

title: Autonomy as Geodesic: Information Geometry of Harness Design
section: 2. The Fisher Information Metric on Configuration Space
text:
2. The Fisher Information Metric on Configuration Space
The central object here is the Fisher information metric (FIM). For the parameter vector \(\theta = (\theta^1, \dots, \theta^n)\), the components are
\[
g_{ij}(\theta) \;=\; \mathbb{E}_{p_\theta}\!\left[\frac{\partial \log p_\theta(\mathbf{y}\mid\mathbf{x})}{\partial \theta^i}\;\frac{\partial \log p_\theta(\mathbf{y}\mid\mathbf{x})}{\partial \theta^j}\right].
\]
In plain terms: \(g_{ij}\) measures how much the agent’s behavioral distribution shifts when you nudge parameter \(i\) and parameter \(j\) at the same time. Think of it as the intrinsic “stiffness” of the harness along the \((i,j)\) direction.
The arc length of a path \(\gamma(t)\), \(t \in [0,1]\), in configuration space works out to
\[
L(\gamma) \;=\; \int_0^1 \sqrt{g_{ij}(\gamma(t))\;\dot{\gamma}^i \dot{\gamma}^j}\; dt.
\]
In plain terms: this is the “effort score” of reconfiguring the harness, measured in units of behavioral change rather than parameter units. A path that changes a lot of parameters but produces little behavioral shift is short; a path that tweaks few parameters but radically alters the agent’s decision boundary is long.
The FIM is positive-definite on the interior of \(\Theta\) (where \(p_\theta\) is regular), so \((\mathcal{M}, g)\) is a genuine Riemannian manifold. The Levi-Civita connection \(\Gamma^i_{jk}\) comes in the standard way, and the geodesic equation reads
\[
\ddot{\gamma}^i + \Gamma^i_{jk}\,\dot{\gamma}^j \dot{\gamma}^k = 0.
\]
Engineering reading. The geodesic equation isn’t some aesthetic choice. It’s the minimum-effort path between two autonomy levels. Any non-geodesic reconfiguration—say, flipping the permission matrix before tightening the verification gate—traverses a longer path and thus incurs more behavioral disruption than strictly necessary. This is the geometric content behind the ordering-sensitivity I observed in Percolation of Autonomy: Critical Dynamics in Harness Design, where autonomy emerges in discrete jumps rather than sliding in continuously.

title: Autonomy as Geodesic: Information Geometry of Harness Design
text:
3. Geodesics as Optimal Autonomy Transitions

Theorem (informal). Let \(\theta_A\) and \(\theta_B\) be two harness configurations at autonomy levels \(\ell_A < \ell_B\) (per the five-level spectrum in The Autonomy Imperative). Among all smooth reconfiguration paths \(\gamma\) with \(\gamma(0)=\theta_A\), \(\gamma(1)=\theta_B\), the geodesic \(\gamma^*\) minimizes the Fisher arc length \(L(\gamma)\). Equivalently, the geodesic is the unique path that maximizes behavioral continuity per unit of parameter change.

The proof is the standard variational argument: the arc-length functional is convex in the velocity \(\dot{\gamma}\) (since \(g_{ij}\) is positive-definite), and the Euler–Lagrange equation yields the geodesic ODE. Uniqueness holds locally (within a convex normal neighborhood), which is exactly the regime in which practical autonomy transitions live.

A Worked 2-D Example
Consider a harness with two free parameters: the mean confidence threshold \(\mu\) and the verification strictness \(\sigma\). The induced outcome model is Gaussian, \(p_\theta(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x}) = \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\). The Fisher information metric is
\[
g_{\mu\mu} = \frac{1}{\sigma^2}, \qquad g_{\mu\sigma} = 0, \qquad g_{\sigma\sigma} = \frac{2}{\sigma^2}.
\]
The Christoffel symbols (non-zero) are:
\[
\Gamma^\mu_{\mu\sigma} = -\frac{1}{2\sigma}, \qquad \Gamma^\sigma_{\mu\mu} = \frac{1}{4\sigma}, \qquad \Gamma^\sigma_{\sigma\sigma} = -\frac{1}{\sigma}.
\]
The geodesic equations become:
\[
\ddot{\mu} - \frac{1}{\sigma}\,\dot{\mu}\,\dot{\sigma} = 0, \qquad \ddot{\sigma} + \frac{1}{2\sigma}\,\dot{\mu}^{\,2} - \frac{2}{\sigma}\,\dot{\sigma}^{\,2} = 0.
\]
Starting at \((\mu, \sigma) = (0, 1)\) with initial velocity \((\dot\mu, \dot\sigma) = (1, 0)\), the first-order expansion gives \(\mu(t) \approx t\), \(\sigma(t) \approx 1 - t^2/4\). The arc length over \(t \in [0, 1]\) is
\[
L \;=\; \int_0^1 \frac{\sqrt{1 + t^2/2}}{1 - t^2/4}\;dt \;\approx\; 1.13.
\]
The sectional curvature of this 2-D surface is constant: \(K = -1/4\).
Engineering reading. A constant negative curvature means that any reconfiguration path between two autonomy levels on this surface will exhibit “divergence”: two initially similar reconfiguration strategies (e.g., “raise \(\mu\) first” vs. “raise \(\sigma\) first”) will separate as the transition proceeds. The negative curvature quantifies how quickly those strategies diverge. In practice, this means that at higher autonomy levels, the ordering of constraint relaxation becomes increasingly consequential—a prediction consistent with the percolation-criticality findings in Percolation of Autonomy.

title: Autonomy as Geodesic: Information Geometry of Harness Design
section: 4. Curvature and the Cost of Autonomy
text:
4. Curvature and the Cost of Autonomy
The Riemann curvature tensor \(R^i_{\;jkl}\) encodes the failure of parallel-transported vectors to close around infinitesimal loops. For engineering purposes, though, what actually matters is the sectional curvature in the 2-plane spanned by two reconfiguration directions \(u, v\):
\[
K(u,v) \;=\; \frac{R_{ikjl}\;u^i v^j v^k u^l}{\bigl(g_{ik}g_{jl} - g_{il}g_{jk}\bigr)\;u^i u^j v^k v^l}.
\]
The denominator is \(\|u\|^2\|v\|^2 - \langle u, v\rangle^2\), which is just the squared area of the parallelogram spanned by \(u\) and \(v\).
Interpretation. If \(K > 0\) in the \((\partial_i, \partial_j)\) plane, then relaxing constraint \(i\) and then \(j\) produces a different final behavioral state than relaxing \(j\) and then \(i\)—the commutator \([\nabla_i, \nabla_j]\) is non-zero. The agent’s interpretation of “safe” or “correct” depends on the path you took. If \(K < 0\) (as in our Gaussian example), the two orderings diverge, and that divergence grows with the magnitude of the reconfiguration.

Corollary (informal). The cost of a non-geodesic reconfiguration exceeds the geodesic cost by an amount proportional to the integral of \(K\) over the 2-surface swept out by the deviation. In the small-deviation limit, the excess cost is \(\tfrac{1}{2}\int K\, dA + O(\epsilon^4)\), where \(dA\) is the area element of the deviation surface.

This is a geometric “free lunch” that is, of course, bounded by the curvature: the more curved the manifold, the more you pay for taking a shortcut.
Engineering reading. Before you relax a pair of constraints simultaneously, compute (or at least estimate) the sectional curvature in that 2-plane. If \(|K|\) is large, sequence the relaxations and re-verify after each step. If \(|K| \approx 0\), the order doesn’t matter and you can parallelize the change. This turns the qualitative heuristic “change one thing at a time” into an actual quantitative decision rule.

title: Autonomy as Geodesic: Information Geometry of Harness Design
text:
5. Parallel Transport and Constraint Inheritance
A constraint in a harness isn’t merely a boolean flag; it carries semantic content—a specification of what the agent should or shouldn’t do, expressed in the coordinate frame of the current autonomy level. When the harness transitions from \(\theta_A\) to \(\theta_B\), the constraint’s meaning has to be transported along the path.
Parallel transport along the geodesic \(\gamma^*\) is defined by the covariant derivative:
\[
\nabla_{\dot{\gamma}} V = 0, \qquad \text{i.e.} \quad \dot{V}^i + \Gamma^i_{jk}\,\dot{\gamma}^j V^k = 0.
\]
The solution \(V(t)\) is the “constraint vector” as seen by the agent at each point along the transition. If the holonomy \(\mathcal{H}(\gamma^*)\)—the net rotation of \(V\) after transporting around a closed loop—vanishes, the constraint semantics are path-independent: the agent’s understanding of “do not write to production” is the same whether you got there via Level 2 or Level 4.
I’d argue this is the geometric content of the dialectic I articulated in Scaffolding to Sovereignty: The Dialectic of Code Autonomy: scaffolding isn’t a tax on autonomy but the generative precondition, because the parallel transport defines what autonomy means at each level. Without the transport structure, “more autonomy” is just “more parameters turned up,” and the semantic content of the constraints dissolves into noise.
Engineering reading. When you promote an agent from “suggest” (Level 2) to “execute” (Level 4), the constraint “respect the project’s style guide” must be re-instantiated in the new autonomy frame. Parallel transport is the mathematical prescription for that re-instantiation. In practice? Re-run the style-check verification gate in the new permission scope, and confirm that the agent’s output distribution (conditioned on the style constraint) hasn’t shifted beyond your tolerance. That’s one step of the transport ODE, discretized.

title: Autonomy as Geodesic: Information Geometry of Harness Design
section: 6. The Geodesic Design Workflow: Six Steps from Current to Target Autonomy
text:
6. The Geodesic Design Workflow: Six Steps from Current to Target Autonomy
All that theory reduces to a concrete engineering procedure. Given a current harness \(\theta_A\) and a target autonomy level \(\ell_B\):



Step
Action
Geometric object




1
Enumerate free parameters; fix gauge (see Gauge Symmetry)
Coordinate chart on \(\mathcal{M}\)


2
Estimate \(g_{ij}\) via Monte Carlo on your task suite \(\mathcal{D}\)
Fisher information metric


3
Compute Christoffel symbols \(\Gamma^i_{jk}\) from \(g_{ij}\)
Levi-Civita connection


4
Solve the geodesic ODE \(\ddot\gamma^i + \Gamma^i_{jk}\dot\gamma^j\dot\gamma^k = 0\) with \(\gamma(0)=\theta_A\), \(\dot\gamma(0)\) chosen toward \(\theta_B\)
Geodesic \(\gamma^*\)


5
Evaluate \(L(\gamma^*)\) (effort) and \(K\) along the path (fragility)
Arc length, sectional curvature


6
Parallel-transport each constraint vector; check holonomy
Constraint semantics



Step 2 in practice. You don’t need the full \(n \times n\) metric. For a harness with \(n \leq 20\) free parameters, a Monte Carlo estimate with \(N = 10^4\) task samples gives \(g_{ij}\) to roughly \(\sim 1\%\) accuracy. The computation is embarrassingly parallel: each sample contributes an outer product \(\nabla_\theta \log p_\theta \otimes \nabla_\theta \log p_\theta\). Libraries like geomstats (Python) or the riemann package (R) provide the geodesic solver and curvature computation out of the box.
Step 4 in practice. The geodesic ODE is a system of \(n\) second-order ODEs. For \(n \leq 20\), a standard Runge-Kutta 4th-order integrator with adaptive step size will do. For larger \(n\), exploit the block-diagonal structure that falls out of modular harness design: scope rules, permissions, verification, and feedback controllers couple only through a small number of shared parameters.
Engineering reading. The workflow replaces the ad-hoc question “should I relax the sandbox first or the verification gate first?” with the computation “what is the geodesic, and what is the curvature in the (sandbox, verification) plane?” The answer is a number, not a gut feeling.

title: Autonomy as Geodesic: Information Geometry of Harness Design
text:
7. Connection to Natural Gradient Descent
The Fisher information metric isn’t a purely geometric abstraction; it’s the metric that makes natural gradient descent (Amari, 1998) invariant to reparameterization. In the harness-design context, this means the following: if you’re tuning a harness (adjusting \(\theta\) to maximize a performance objective \(J(\theta)\)), the natural gradient
\[
\tilde{\nabla} J = g^{-1} \nabla J
\]
is the steepest-ascent direction in behavioral space, not in parameter space. A unit step in the natural-gradient direction produces the same behavioral change regardless of how you happen to parameterize the harness.
This connection isn’t incidental. The rate-distortion cost floor I derived in The Autonomy Channel can be re-expressed as a bound on the natural-gradient step size: the maximum autonomy increment per tuning iteration is limited by the Fisher-information budget, which is precisely the free-energy bound I quantified in Free Energy Bounds: A Variational Account of Autonomy. The geodesic framework unifies these results: the geodesic is the path of constant natural-gradient step size, and its length is the total Fisher-information budget consumed by the transition.
Engineering reading. If you’ve been tuning your harness with grid search or random search over parameter values, you’re working in a coordinate-dependent metric. Switching to natural-gradient updates (or, equivalently, to geodesic interpolation) makes your tuning invariant to how you choose to parameterize the harness. The same behavioral improvement requires the same number of iterations, whether you express the threshold as a probability, a log-odds, or a percentile.

title: Autonomy as Geodesic: Information Geometry of Harness Design
text:
8. Limitations
Three caveats worth keeping in mind.
First: the outcome model is a projection. The distribution \(p_\theta(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x})\) captures only the observable behavioral signature of the harness. Internal state, prompt engineering, and model-specific quirks (say, a particular LLM’s sensitivity to instruction phrasing) aren’t encoded in the manifold. The Fisher metric is therefore a lower bound on the true reconfiguration cost: it measures the cost of the observable change, not the cost of the internal reorganization that produces it.
Second: the manifold may be singular. At the boundary of \(\Theta\) (e.g., zero verification strictness, or a fully open sandbox), the FIM can become degenerate. The geometry goes singular, and geodesics may not exist or may not be unique. In practice, this corresponds to the “cliff” configurations where a small parameter change produces a discontinuous behavioral shift—precisely the percolation-critical regime identified in Percolation of Autonomy.
Third: the computational cost scales with \(n^3\). Estimating and inverting the Fisher metric for \(n > 100\) parameters is non-trivial. Modular harness design (keeping \(n \leq 30\) per module) and the gauge reduction from Gauge Symmetry are the practical mitigations. For very large harnesses, a local (tangent-space) approximation to the metric is usually sufficient, since autonomy transitions are typically short-horizon.

title: Autonomy as Geodesic: Information Geometry of Harness Design
text:
A Closing Note
The geodesic stands as a regulative ideal. The harness engineer who computes the Fisher metric, solves the geodesic ODE, and checks the holonomy isn’t performing a ritual. They’re making the implicit costs of autonomy transitions explicit, comparable, and optimizable. The geometry doesn’t eliminate engineering judgment—it gives judgment a coordinate system.
If you’re building a harness and want to try estimating the Fisher metric on your task suite, the six-step workflow in Section 6 is a reasonable starting point. I’d genuinely be interested to hear whether the predicted cost floor matches your observed engineering effort. And if the geodesic length disagrees with your intuition about “how hard it is to add another autonomy level”? That discrepancy is itself a diagnostic: it means your parameterization is hiding degrees of freedom, or your outcome model is too coarse.
— Author’s note: This post is Part 7 in an incremental series on building a fully autonomous coding-agent harness. Previous parts cover the autonomy spectrum (Part 1), the Shannon-channel model (Part 2), the scaffolding dialectic (Part 3), percolation dynamics (Part 4), gauge reduction (Part 5), and free-energy bounds (Part 6). The next installment will apply the geodesic workflow to a concrete SDLC-phase transition (specification → implementation) with a worked template.

title: Autonomy as Ergodicity: Mixing Theorems for Harness Design
text: TL;DR — We recast complete autonomy in a coding-agent harness as ergodicity of its state dynamics. The payoff is three concrete, CI-auditable numbers: a polynomial mixing-time bound \(t_{\text{mix}} = O(N^2/\delta)\) that tells you the worst-case ticks to full task coverage; a KAM perturbation threshold \(\varepsilon_{\max}\) bounding how many constraints you can add before autonomy breaks; and a linear program whose solution is the maximal-autonomy invariant measure. If you are building a ReAct-style or plan-act harness, these three numbers are the ones to compute before your next release.

title: Autonomy as Ergodicity: Mixing Theorems for Harness Design
text:
Abstract
We model the coding-agent harness as a measure-preserving transformation \(T\) on a finite state space \(\Omega\) of \(N\) discrete harness configurations (tool selections, context windows, permission states, and loop phases). We define complete autonomy as the ergodicity of \(T\): the irreducibility of the dynamics into a single invariant component, so that no proper subset of states is closed under the dynamics. Under this definition, we prove a polynomial mixing-time bound of the form \(t_{\text{mix}} \leq C\, N^2 / \delta\), where \(\delta\) is the spectral gap of the associated transition matrix and \(C\) is a universal constant. We then apply Kolmogorov–Arnold–Moser (KAM) perturbation theory to show that additive constraint perturbations of magnitude \(\varepsilon < \varepsilon_{\max}(\delta, N)\) preserve the ergodic structure, yielding a certifiable robustness margin. Finally, we formulate an ergodic-optimization linear program whose solution identifies the invariant measure \(\mu^*\) maximizing an autonomy objective (task-coverage entropy). Together, these results convert the qualitative question “is my agent autonomous?” into three quantitative, CI-auditable checks.
Why this matters. Let’s be honest about where harness evaluation stands right now. We’ve got benchmark scores everywhere—SWE-bench pass@k, AgentBench success rates, τ-bench trajectory fidelity—and they all measure outcome autonomy. Did the agent finish the task? Nice. But none of them bound the process autonomy: the guarantee that the agent will, within a computable number of steps, actually explore every relevant configuration rather than silently collapsing into some degenerate attractor it found early on. The ergodicity framework fills exactly that gap. It hands you a structural certificate, not a behavioral statistic. And that’s a fundamentally different thing to have in your CI pipeline.

Prerequisites
You’ll want some familiarity with finite-state Markov chains (transition matrices, stationary distributions, spectral decomposition), basic measure-preserving dynamics (ergodicity, invariant sets), and the ReAct / plan-act harness loop. No knowledge of symplectic geometry or KAM theory is required—we state only the corollary we use, and I’ll explain it in plain terms.

title: Autonomy as Ergodicity: Mixing Theorems for Harness Design
section: 1. Why Ergodicity Is the Right Invariant for Agent Autonomy
text:
1. Why Ergodicity Is the Right Invariant for Agent Autonomy

1.1 The state space
A coding-agent harness at any given moment is characterized by a tuple
\[
s = (c,\; \tau,\; \pi,\; \phi) \in \Omega,
\]
where \(c\) is the active context window (or a hash thereof), \(\tau\) is the selected tool or action, \(\pi\) is the permission/authorization state, and \(\phi\) is the loop phase (plan, act, observe, reflect). In a well-factored harness, \(\Omega\) is finite: \(|\Omega| = N\) for some \(N\) in the range \(10^1\)–\(10^4\) depending on tool count and phase granularity.
The harness transition \(T: \Omega \to \Omega\) is the deterministic (or stochastic, if the LLM sampling introduces entropy) map that takes the current configuration to the next. In the deterministic case, \(T\) is just a permutation of \(\Omega\); in the stochastic case, we work with the associated Markov kernel \(P(s, s') = \Pr[T(s') \mid s]\).


1.2 Defining autonomy as ergodicity
Definition 1 (Complete Autonomy). A harness \(T\) with state space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mu)\) is fully autonomous if and only if \(T\) is ergodic with respect to the uniform measure \(\mu\): for every measurable set \(A \subseteq \Omega\) satisfying \(T^{-1}(A) = A\) (i.e., \(A\) is invariant), either \(\mu(A) = 0\) or \(\mu(A) = 1\).
In plain language: there is no non-trivial “cage” of states the agent can get trapped in. The agent’s dynamics don’t fragment into disconnected behavioral modes. If \(T\) has two disjoint invariant sets \(A\) and \(B\), the agent is not autonomous—it has silently chosen a personality (always uses tool X, never enters the reflect phase, etc.) and will never, ever leave it. You’d never know unless you checked.
And here’s the thing: this definition is deliberately stronger than “the agent completes the task.” A task-completing agent might pass through only 5 of 120 states, ignoring the rest entirely. Ergodicity demands that all states are reachable in the long run. That’s the structural guarantee you actually want before you pull the human out of the loop.


1.3 Relation to prior work in the series
The five-level autonomy spectrum in The Autonomy Imperative gives us the qualitative ladder; ergodicity gives the top rung a rigorous predicate. The spectral-gap analysis in The Spectral Gap of Autonomy computes the convergence speed \(\delta\) that shows up as a parameter in our mixing bound. The percolation threshold in Percolation of Autonomy identifies the constraint density at which the invariant set fragments—precisely the point where ergodicity is lost. Our KAM certificate (§3) is the local-robustness companion to that global percolation picture.

title: Autonomy as Ergodicity: Mixing Theorems for Harness Design
section: 2. Polynomial Mixing-Time Bound: A Quantitative Latency Certificate
text:
2. Polynomial Mixing-Time Bound: A Quantitative Latency Certificate

2.1 The theorem
Let \(P\) be the \(N \times N\) stochastic transition matrix of the harness, with eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 = 1, \lambda_2, \dots, \lambda_N\). Define the spectral gap
\[
\delta \;=\; 1 - \max_{i \geq 2} |\lambda_i|.
\]
Theorem 2 (Mixing-Time Bound). If \(P\) is aperiodic and irreducible, then the \(\varepsilon\)-mixing time satisfies
\[
t_{\text{mix}}(\varepsilon) \;\leq\; \frac{1}{\delta}\,\ln\!\frac{1}{\varepsilon\, \pi_{\min}},
\]
where \(\pi_{\min} = \min_s \pi(s)\) is the smallest stationary probability. In particular, for \(\varepsilon = 1/N\) (uniform accuracy) and \(\pi_{\min} \geq 1/N\),
\[
\boxed{\;t_{\text{mix}} \;\leq\; \frac{N}{\delta}\,\ln N\; = \; O\!\left(\frac{N^2}{\delta}\right).}
\]
Sketch. The bound follows by decomposing \(P^t - \pi\mathbf{1}^T\) into its spectral components. The dominant non-trivial term decays as \(|\lambda_2|^t = e^{-\delta t}\) (up to sub-exponential factors from Jordan blocks, which are bounded by a polynomial in \(N\) for stochastic matrices via Weyl’s inequality applied to the symmetric part of \(P\)). Setting \(|\lambda_2|^t \leq \varepsilon\,\pi_{\min}\) and solving for \(t\) gives the stated bound. The \(N^2\) dependence arises from the worst-case \(\pi_{\min} = 1/N\) and the \(\ln N\) factor.


2.2 What this means for your harness
Okay, so now you actually have a CI-auditable latency guarantee. Before you ship a harness configuration, you can compute \(N\) (count your states), estimate \(\delta\) (run the spectral-conditioning algorithm from The Spectral Gap of Autonomy), and get a concrete upper bound on the number of ticks the agent needs before its behavior is statistically indistinguishable from the invariant measure.
Here’s the part that should get your attention: if \(t_{\text{mix}}\) exceeds your SLA (say, 10 000 tokens), you know a priori that the harness is structurally too slow. Not because the LLM is slow. Because the state space is poorly connected. That’s a design problem, not a model problem, and it means you can fix it without swapping models.


2.3 Worked example: a 12-state ReAct harness
Consider a harness with \(N = 12\) states: 4 phases (plan, act, observe, reflect) × 3 tool tiers (local, sandboxed, production). The transition matrix \(P\) is built from the ReAct loop: from any act state, the agent moves to observe; from observe, it probabilistically routes to plan (with probability 0.7) or reflect (0.3); from plan, it routes to act (1.0); from reflect, it routes to plan (0.8) or terminates (0.2, which we treat as a self-loop on the plan state for ergodicity purposes).
Suppose a numerical eigendecomposition yields \(\lambda_2 = 0.95\), so \(\delta = 0.05\). Then:
\[
t_{\text{mix}} \;\leq\; \frac{12}{0.05}\,\ln 12 \;\approx\; 240 \times 2.485 \;\approx\; 596 \text{ ticks}.
\]
If your harness runs at 50 tokens/tick, that’s a 29 800-token worst-case exploration budget. Now, if your task SLA is 20 000 tokens, you’ve got a problem. The harness is structurally too slow at \(\delta = 0.05\). You need to either reduce \(N\) (merge tool tiers) or increase \(\delta\) (add more cross-phase transitions). Either way, you know before you hit production.

title: Autonomy as Ergodicity: Mixing Theorems for Harness Design
section: 3. KAM Perturbation Certificate: How Much Constraint Can You Add?
text:
3. KAM Perturbation Certificate: How Much Constraint Can You Add?

3.1 The problem
In practice, nobody designs a harness in one shot. You start with a permissive core and incrementally bolt on constraints: a security policy that blocks rm -rf, a UI constraint that forces the agent to render diffs before committing, a spec checklist that gates the reflect phase. Each addition is a perturbation \(\Delta P\) to the transition matrix: \(P' = P + \Delta P\).
The question that keeps me up at night: how large can \(\|\Delta P\|\) be before ergodicity is destroyed?


3.2 The KAM certificate
The full KAM theorem (Kolmogorov, 1954; Arnold, 1963; Moser, 1962) concerns near-integrable Hamiltonian systems and is, frankly, overkill here. We use only the following corollary, which is a direct consequence of the implicit-function theorem applied to the eigenvalue equation:
Theorem 3 (Ergodicity Preservation under Perturbation). Let \(P\) be an \(N \times N\) irreducible, aperiodic stochastic matrix with spectral gap \(\delta > 0\). Let \(P' = P + \Delta\) where \(\Delta\) is a perturbation preserving row-stochasticity. If
\[
\|\Delta\|_{\infty} \;<\; \varepsilon_{\max} \;=\; \frac{\delta}{2\,(N-1)},
\]
then \(P'\) is also irreducible and aperiodic, and its spectral gap satisfies \(\delta' \geq \delta - 2N\|\Delta\|_{\infty}\).
Intuition (the “moat” picture). Think of the eigenvalue \(\lambda_1 = 1\) as an island and the remaining eigenvalues as points scattered in the complex plane. The spectral gap \(\delta\) is the width of the “moat” separating the island from the nearest point. A perturbation of magnitude \(\varepsilon\) shifts each eigenvalue by at most \(N\varepsilon\) (Gershgorin). If \(N\varepsilon < \delta/2\), no eigenvalue can cross the moat; the island stays isolated; irreducibility is preserved. In short: the gap is a moat, and a perturbation smaller than the moat width cannot bridge it.


3.3 Practical KAM budget
For the 12-state example above (\(\delta = 0.05\), \(N = 12\)):
\[
\varepsilon_{\max} = \frac{0.05}{2 \times 11} \approx 0.00227.
\]
This means: each row of \(\Delta P\) can have \(L^1\) mass at most \(\approx 0.23\%\) redistributed. Concretely? If you add a security gate that diverts 5% of act/prod transitions to a blocked state, you are exceeding the KAM threshold by more than 20×. Ergodicity is not guaranteed; the agent may now be trapped in the blocked attractor. You added one safety check and broke the whole system.
What this means for your harness. Before adding any constraint, compute \(\varepsilon_{\max}\) from your current \(\delta\) and \(N\). If the constraint’s transition-mass shift exceeds \(\varepsilon_{\max}\), you’ve got three options: (a) reduce the constraint’s strength, (b) add compensating transitions to restore the gap, or (c) accept the loss of ergodicity and redesign the state space. This is a certifiable, per-constraint budget check that can run in a CI pipeline in \(O(N^3)\) time (one eigendecomposition). Five minutes of compute. Worth it.


3.4 The aperiodicity trade-off
The theorems above require aperiodicity (\(\gcd\) of return-time periods = 1). In practice, a ReAct loop with fixed phase ordering (plan → act → observe → plan) is periodic with period 3. A common fix is to add a small stochastic “skip” (e.g., 5% probability of staying in the same phase).
Does this break task-completion guarantees? No. But it does increase \(t_{\text{mix}}\) by a factor of at most \((1-\alpha)^{-1}\) where \(\alpha\) is the skip probability. At \(\alpha = 0.05\), the overhead is ≈ 6%. The structural benefit (aperiodicity, hence applicability of the mixing bound) far outweighs a 6% latency cost. Honestly, this is the single cheapest ergodicity fix available. Add the skip, move on.

title: Autonomy as Ergodicity: Mixing Theorems for Harness Design
section: 4. Ergodic Optimization: Finding the Maximal-Autonomy Measure
text:
4. Ergodic Optimization: Finding the Maximal-Autonomy Measure

4.1 The problem
Given a harness \(P\) that is ergodic, there’s a unique stationary distribution \(\pi\). But here’s where it gets interesting: you may have design freedom. The transition probabilities within each phase are not fixed by the LLM—they’re set by your harness code (routing rules, tool-selection heuristics, context-window management). So the question becomes:

Among all stochastic matrices \(P\) consistent with your architectural constraints (e.g., phase ordering, security gates), which \(P\) maximizes an autonomy objective?

A natural objective is the task-coverage entropy:
\[
\mathcal{H}(\pi) = -\sum_{s \in \Omega} \pi(s) \log \pi(s).
\]
Maximizing \(\mathcal{H}(\pi)\) pushes the stationary distribution toward uniformity, which is the ergodic “ideal”: the agent spends equal long-run time in every configuration. No state is starved.


4.2 The linear program
The entropy-maximization is nonlinear, but the constraint set is linear, and the objective is concave, so the problem is a convex program. For a blog-level implementation, the LP relaxation (linearizing the entropy via its tangent at the uniform distribution) is sufficient and gives the same optimal vertex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{maximize} \quad & \sum_s \pi(s) \quad \text{(subject to } \pi \geq 0,\; \mathbf{1}^T\pi = 1) \\
\text{subject to} \quad & \pi P = \pi \\
& P \geq 0, \quad \mathbf{1}^T P = \mathbf{1} \quad \text{(row-stochastic)} \\
& P_{ij} \leq \bar{p}_{ij} \quad \text{(architectural upper bounds)} \\
& P_{ij} \geq \underline{p}_{ij} \quad \text{(security lower bounds)}
\end{aligned}
\]


4.3 A 5-line Python sketch
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import linprog

N = 5  # toy state space
# c: objective (maximize uniformity → minimize -sum π)
c = np.ones(N)
# A_eq: π P = π  →  (P^T - I) π = 0, plus sum(π) = 1
P = np.full((N, N), 1/N)  # start from uniform (feasible)
A_eq = np.vstack([np.hstack([P.T - np.eye(N), np.zeros(N)]),
                  np.ones(2 * N)])
b_eq = np.concatenate([np.zeros(N), [1.0]])
res = linprog(c, A_eq=A_eq, b_eq=b_eq, bounds=[(0, 1)] * N)
print("Optimal π:", res.x)
This is a toy, obviously. The production version replaces the fixed \(P\) with decision variables and adds the architectural bounds \(\bar{p}_{ij}\), \(\underline{p}_{ij}\). The solver (HiGHS, Gurobi, or even cvxpy) returns the maximal-autonomy stationary distribution in milliseconds for \(N \leq 10^4\). You’ll barely notice it running.


4.4 Relation to the free-energy bound
The ergodic LP is the constrained version of the variational free-energy bound developed in Free Energy Bounds: A Variational Account of Autonomy. Over there, the KL budget per step is the dual variable; here, the architectural bounds \(\bar{p}_{ij}\) play the same role. The two formulations are Fenchel-dual: the LP is the primal (choose transitions), the free-energy bound is the dual (pay a KL cost for deviation from the prior). For practitioners, I’d say the LP is the more actionable object. You can actually run it.

title: Autonomy as Ergodicity: Mixing Theorems for Harness Design
section: 5. Common Harness Design Pitfalls (and How to Fix Them)
text:
5. Common Harness Design Pitfalls (and How to Fix Them)
The following mistakes show up repeatedly in production harnesses, and they’re all diagnosable by the three numbers above (\(N\), \(\delta\), \(\varepsilon_{\max}\)):



#
Pitfall
Symptom
Diagnostic
Fix




1
Phase lock. The agent always cycles plan→act→observe and never enters reflect.
\(\delta\) is small; a 3-state cycle is an invariant set.
Check \(\gcd\) of return times; verify aperiodicity.
Add a 5% stochastic skip (§3.4).


2
Tool-tier collapse. The agent selects the local tier 98% of the time, ignoring sandbox and production.
\(\pi_{\min} \approx 0.005\); mixing time explodes.
Compute \(\pi\); check entropy \(\mathcal{H}(\pi)\).
Add a context-dependent routing rule that forces tier escalation on specific error patterns.


3
Security over-constraint. A new rm -rf block creates a blocked state with no outgoing edge.
\(P\) loses irreducibility; \(\delta \to 0\).
Run the KAM check: \(\|\Delta P\|_\infty > \varepsilon_{\max}\).
Add a “retry with confirmation” transition out of the blocked state.


4
Context-window starvation. The context hash \(c\) has \(10^6\) possible values, making \(N\) enormous.
\(t_{\text{mix}}\) is infeasible.
Coarse-grain \(c\) (see Coarse-Graining Autonomy).
Reduce \(N\) via RG flow; keep only the top-\(k\) context buckets.


5
Silent attractor. A rare error path (e.g., a 429 rate-limit) sends the agent into a retry loop that never exits.
A 2-state invariant subset exists.
Ergodicity test: find \(A \subset \Omega\) with \(P(A, A) = 1\).
Add a max-retry counter that forces transition to reflect.



Each row is a 5-minute CI check: compute \(N\), run the eigendecomposition, verify \(\delta > 0\) and \(\|\Delta P\|_\infty < \varepsilon_{\max}\). If any check fails, the harness is not structurally autonomous. And I mean that no matter how well it scores on SWE-bench. A 95th-percentile benchmark score means nothing if the agent is stuck in a 3-state loop.

title: Autonomy as Ergodicity: Mixing Theorems for Harness Design
section: 6. Positioning: How This Relates to SWE-bench, AgentBench, and τ-bench
text:
6. Positioning: How This Relates to SWE-bench, AgentBench, and τ-bench
The dominant agent-evaluation frameworks measure behavioral autonomy:

SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., 2023): pass@k on real GitHub issues. Measures outcome success.
AgentBench (Liu et al., 2023): multi-task success across web, OS, DB environments. Measures task coverage.
τ-bench (Yao et al., 2024): trajectory-level fidelity to a reference policy. Measures process similarity.

None of them answer the structural question: “Is the agent’s state dynamics ergodic? Will it, in the long run, explore all of its configuration space, or is it silently stuck in a subset?” A SWE-bench pass@1 of 30% is perfectly compatible with an agent that only uses 3 of its 12 states. You’d never know from the benchmark. The ergodicity certificate is orthogonal to these benchmarks: it’s a necessary (not sufficient) condition for genuine autonomy. I’d recommend running the ergodicity check as a pre-gate in the CI pipeline, before the benchmark suite is even invoked.
The rate-distortion cost floor in The Autonomy Channel gives you the information-theoretic lower bound on the distortion a harness must accept; the ergodicity bound gives you the temporal upper bound on how long convergence takes. Together, they bracket the design space: you cannot simultaneously minimize distortion and minimize mixing time below the product of the two lower bounds. That’s a hard wall.

title: Autonomy as Ergodicity: Mixing Theorems for Harness Design
section: 7. How to Build \(P\) from Your ReAct Loop (Practical Guide)
text:
7. How to Build \(P\) from Your ReAct Loop (Practical Guide)
The theorems assume you have the transition matrix \(P\). In practice, you have to extract it from harness code. Three steps:

Enumerate states. Walk your harness source. Each distinct combination of (phase, tool-tier, permission-level) is one state. For a typical ReAct harness with 4 phases, 3 tool tiers, and 2 permission levels, \(N = 24\). Write this as a constant in your config: HARNESS_N = 24.
Extract transitions. For each state \(s\), trace the control flow to identify the next state \(s'\) and the probability (if stochastic) or the deterministic target. In a plan-act harness, this is usually a hardcoded routing table. Encode it as an \(N \times N\) matrix. If the LLM sampling introduces stochasticity, estimate \(P_{ij}\) from a 1 000-episode trace.
Validate. Check row-stochasticity (\(\sum_j P_{ij} = 1\) for all \(i\)), verify irreducibility (all states reachable), and compute \(\delta\) via numpy.linalg.eigvals(P.T). If \(\delta \approx 0\), you have an invariant subset—go back to step 2 and figure out where the disconnect is.

This is the same procedure as the spectral-conditioning algorithm in The Spectral Gap of Autonomy, extended with the KAM check and the ergodic LP.

text:
8. How This Fits the Series
This post is the ergodic-theoretic core of the harness-autonomy series. It sits at the intersection of several prior results:

Scaffolding to Sovereignty provides the dialectical framing: scaffolding is the generative precondition for autonomy, not its enemy. The KAM certificate is the quantitative version of this claim—small scaffolds (constraints) preserve the ergodic core.
Gauge Symmetry and the Invariant Core identifies the inequivalent autonomy structures; ergodicity is the invariant that survives gauge transformations.
Functorial Autonomy gives the categorical criterion for safe refactoring; the KAM certificate is the analytic version of the same check.
Cohomological Obstructions proves that some failures are topological; ergodicity failure is the simplest topological obstruction (a non-trivial invariant set is a 0-dimensional cohomology class).
Canalized Autonomy computes basin depth; the spectral gap \(\delta\) is the flatness of the basin floor.
Autonomy as Geodesic measures the effort of autonomy transitions; \(t_{\text{mix}}\) measures the time.

title: Autonomy as Ergodicity: Mixing Theorems for Harness Design
section: 9. Next Steps: Three Numbers to Compute Before Your Next Release
text:
9. Next Steps: Three Numbers to Compute Before Your Next Release
If you’re building a coding-agent harness and want a CI-auditable autonomy certificate, here are the three numbers to compute. Seriously, just these three:

\(N\) — the state-space cardinality. Count your (phase, tool, permission) tuples. Target: \(N \leq 100\) (beyond that, coarse-grain via RG flow).
\(\delta\) — the spectral gap. Run np.linalg.eigvals(P.T); take \(1 - \max|\lambda_i|\) for \(i \geq 2\). Target: \(\delta \geq 0.05\) (gives \(t_{\text{mix}} \leq 200\,N\ln N\)).
\(\varepsilon_{\max}\) — the KAM threshold. Compute \(\delta / (2(N-1))\). Every new constraint must satisfy \(\|\Delta P\|_\infty < \varepsilon_{\max}\).

A 10-line script to get started:
import numpy as np

def autonomy_certificate(P: np.ndarray) -> dict:
    N = P.shape[0]
    evals = np.linalg.eigvals(P.T)
    delta = 1.0 - np.max(np.abs(evals[1:]))
    t_mix = N / delta * np.log(N)
    eps_max = delta / (2 * (N - 1))
    return {"N": N, "delta": round(delta, 6),
            "t_mix_ticks": int(t_mix),
            "eps_max": round(eps_max, 8)}
Run this in your CI pipeline on every harness-config change. If \(\delta\) drops below your threshold, the build fails with a message identifying the invariant subset (via a simple graph-reachability check on the transition digraph). No ambiguity. No “it worked in my local test.” Just a number that went below a line.

title: Autonomy as Ergodicity: Mixing Theorems for Harness Design
text:
Discussion
The ergodicity framework has limitations, and it’s worth stating them plainly. First, it’s a necessary but not sufficient condition for autonomy: an ergodic harness can still produce poor code if the LLM’s per-step quality is low. Ergodicity guarantees exploration, not exploitation. Those are different things, and this framework only handles the former.
Second, the finite-state assumption is an idealization. A production harness with a continuous context window is not literally finite-state, but the coarse-graining results in Coarse-Graining Autonomy justify the discretization to within a computable error. Good enough for engineering purposes.
Third, the KAM certificate is a local result. It certifies that a small perturbation preserves ergodicity, but it does not tell you what happens at a large perturbation (say, replacing the entire tool layer). For that, the percolation analysis in Percolation of Autonomy is the right tool.
But the deeper methodological point—and this is what I find genuinely exciting—is that autonomy, far from being some philosophical or behavioral property, is a structural one. It’s a property of the transition matrix, not of the LLM weights. That reframing is what makes it CI-auditable, what makes it amenable to perturbation analysis, and what makes the entire series of posts—spectral, percolative, cohomological, geometric—cohere into a single design calculus. You can put a number on it. You can test it in a pipeline. And that changes everything about how you reason about agent reliability.

title: Autonomy as Ergodicity: Mixing Theorems for Harness Design
text:
Related Posts in This Series

The Spectral Gap of Autonomy: Eigenmodes in Harness Design — Compute the convergence speed \(\delta\) and run the spectral-conditioning algorithm that feeds directly into the mixing bound above.
Percolation of Autonomy: Critical Dynamics in Harness Design — Find the constraint density at which the invariant set fragments; the global complement to the local KAM certificate.
Free Energy Bounds: A Variational Account of Autonomy — The dual (KL-budget) formulation of the ergodic LP; useful when you want a per-step cost model rather than a global stationary distribution.
Cohomological Obstructions to Complete Harness Autonomy — Diagnose why a harness fails the ergodicity test: is the obstruction parametric (fixable by tuning) or topological (requires structural redesign)?
Wasserstein Autonomy: Optimal Transport of Harness States — Quantify the refactoring effort to move from a current non-ergodic configuration to the ergodic target, with a CI-auditable transport plan.


The three numbers—\(N\), \(\delta\), \(\varepsilon_{\max}\)—are the ergonomic handles on harness autonomy. Compute them, log them, and let your CI pipeline enforce them. Everything else in the series is a refinement of one of these three.

title: The Autonomy Imperative: Code as Self-Governing Architecture
text:
Key Takeaways - Autonomy in coding agents isn’t a light switch—it’s a graded spectrum (L1–L5) of architectural self-sufficiency. - Each level is bounded by a verification mechanism; pull that out and the level degrades into uncontrolled delegation. - The tools you’re probably using right now (Cursor, Devin, SWE-agent) sit somewhere in L2–L4 territory. L5? That’s still a design target, not something you can pip install. - The agent harness—that orchestration layer sitting between the LLM and your SDLC—has to be designed for a target autonomy level. You can’t just bolt it on later.
So here’s what this post is actually doing: tracing the theoretical and methodological lineage behind harness-coding practices. At each step along that lineage, a little more decision-making authority shifts from the human operator to the system under construction. The core claim I want to land is this—autonomy in coding agents (AI systems that generate, validate, and ship code with varying degrees of human oversight) is not a binary endpoint. It’s a spectrum. And I’m drawing on control theory, formal verification, and the philosophy of mind to argue that a well-designed agent harness (the orchestration layer that mediates between a large language model and the software development life cycle, or SDLC) can progressively internalize the decision-making functions that used to be exclusively human.
This post sits within a broader series where we build, layer by layer, a fully autonomous coding-agent harness. Each installment adds something: SDLC phase integration, security constraints, UI guardrails, spec-compliance checklists, failure-recovery policies. This one supplies the conceptual scaffolding those practical layers will rest on.

title: The Autonomy Imperative: Code as Self-Governing Architecture
section: The Autonomy Spectrum: Five Levels of Delegation
text:
The Autonomy Spectrum: Five Levels of Delegation
Here’s the thing about calling a system “autonomous.” It’s either a threshold you pass or you don’t, right? Or so the marketing copy suggests. But a more useful framing is a continuum. Five levels capture the progression pretty well:

L1 — Syntax Translation. The model takes a human-specified instruction and spits out syntactically valid code. The human still chooses what to build, how to structure it, and whether the output is actually acceptable. Think of it as a typewriter with a thesaurus attached.
L2 — Local Validation. Now the system generates code and runs a scoped check—unit test, linter, type checker—before handing it back. Delegation extends to “is this locally correct?” but not to “is this the right thing to build?”
L3 — Task-Level Planning. You give it a task description, and it decomposes that into sub-tasks, picks tools, sequences operations, and iterates on partial failures. The human provides the goal and reviews the result. This is where most current coding agents—Cursor, GitHub Copilot Workspace, Devin—live in their standard configurations.
L4 — Project-Level Orchestration. The system manages a multi-file, multi-session project: it maintains a working hypothesis about architecture, coordinates with other agents or services, updates its own task graph in response to integration failures, and produces a reviewable diff with a justification narrative. The human is auditor, not director.
L5 — Self-Governing Architecture. The system ingests a product-level specification, determines which SDLC phases to execute, allocates its own compute budget, selects and composes its own verification strategies, and ships to a staging environment. The human’s role shrinks to setting the specification and adjudicating edge cases that the system flags as below its confidence threshold.

  L2 --> L3["L3\nTask-Level Planning"]

  L4 --> L5["L5\nSelf-Governing"]

And here’s the critical observation that I keep coming back to: each transition is not a matter of “more of the same.” Moving from L2 to L3 requires a fundamentally different verification architecture—local type-checking simply cannot validate a multi-step plan. Moving from L4 to L5 requires the system to select its own verification strategies, which is a meta-cognitive act that no current production system performs reliably. At least, not without a human holding the leash.
