title: Gauge Symmetry and the Invariant Core of Harness Autonomy
text:
I spent three weeks A/B-testing pipeline topologies for an autonomous coding agent. Reordering tool-call stages. Swapping where the verification gate sits. Nudging context-window allocations by a token here, a budget unit there. And you know what? The performance delta was noise. Pure, unremarkable, “is-this-significant-or-is-my-laptop-just-thermal-throttling” noise.
Every “improvement” I measured was, in retrospect, a coordinate artifact. The agent’s actual autonomy structure hadn’t budged. I’d just reparameterized it. Spun the same object on a different axis and called it progress.
This post is my attempt to explain why that frustration is systemic, not just a bad week. Most of the combinatorial explosion in LLM agent harness design is what physicists would call gauge redundancy: architecturally distinct descriptions that are empirically identical. Electromagnetism lets you pick infinitely many vector potentials \(\mathbf{A}\) for the same field \(\mathbf{F} = d\mathbf{A}\). A given autonomy structure, I’ll argue, admits a whole continuous family of harness configurations that differ only in bookkeeping. The thing that actually determines whether your agent succeeds or fails—the curvature, the commutator structure that no amount of reparameterization can scrub away—is what matters.

title: Gauge Symmetry and the Invariant Core of Harness Autonomy
text:
Abstract
There’s a persistent, low-grade frustration in engineering autonomous coding-agent harnesses: the apparent combinatorial freedom in pipeline topology, tool ordering, context allocation, constraint placement. It makes the design space feel infinite when it, I think, isn’t. Drawing on the gauge-symmetry principle from theoretical physics, this post formalizes the “gauge group” \(\mathcal{G}\) of harness reparameterizations, identifies the gauge-invariant autonomy curvature \(\mathcal{K}_{ij}\), and derives design consequences that collapse the effective search space to a finite set of inequivalent configurations. For a harness with \(m\) decision stages, the number of genuinely distinct autonomy structures is bounded by a small number of discrete invariants, regardless of how much continuous reparameterization freedom you have. The practical upshot: classify before you configure.

title: Gauge Symmetry and the Invariant Core of Harness Autonomy
text:
TL;DR — Key Takeaways

Most harness “choices” are gauge artifacts. Reordering tool calls, shifting verification gates, re-allocating context windows—these often describe the same autonomy structure in different coordinates. You’re spinning the same object.
The invariant is the commutator. The gauge-invariant quantity is the autonomy curvature \(\mathcal{K}_{ij}\)—how much the order in which you apply two design knobs actually matters. You can’t transform this away.
The effective design space is finite. For \(m\) decision stages, the number of inequivalent configurations is bounded by a small set of discrete invariants (commutation class, topological winding, budget partition), not by the continuous parameter space.
Classify before you configure. First identify the invariant class of your harness, then optimize within that class. The search shrinks from an infinite continuum to a finite combinatorial problem.
This is tool-agnostic. LangGraph state graphs, CrewAI task DAGs, AutoGen conversation topologies, your bespoke pipeline in a for loop—same invariants. They’re structural, not implementation-specific.

You should be comfortable with basic differential geometry (forms, connections, curvature) and have hands-on experience building LLM agent pipelines. No prior QFT knowledge needed; I’ll introduce the physics analogies as we go.

title: Gauge Symmetry and the Invariant Core of Harness Autonomy
text:
1. The Combinatorial Illusion
Picture a typical autonomous coding agent harness: a sequence of \(m\) decision stages (plan → retrieve → generate → verify → iterate), each with a continuous “knob” turned by some engineer (temperature, context-window size, tool-call budget, retry threshold). A naive read of the design space gives you dimension \(O(m \cdot k)\) where \(k\) is knobs per stage. The implied search space is a high-dimensional hypercube. Intimidating. And—as my three weeks of shuffling made painfully clear—largely wasted effort.
Here’s the key observation, borrowed (heavily) from gauge theory: many points in that hypercube are the same physical point. In electrodynamics, the vector potential \(\mathbf{A}\) is not unique. The gauge transformation \(\mathbf{A} \mapsto \mathbf{A} + \nabla\chi\) leaves the measurable field \(\mathbf{F} = \nabla \times \mathbf{A}\) untouched. The redundancy isn’t a bug in the description; it’s a symmetry. A feature.
I’m claiming an analogous structure exists for agent harnesses. A harness reparameterization is a smooth, invertible remapping of stage orderings, knob allocations, constraint placements that leaves the observable autonomy behavior invariant. All such reparameterizations form a group \(\mathcal{G}\), and the true design space is the quotient \(\mathcal{C}/\mathcal{G}\), where \(\mathcal{C}\) is the space of all configurations.
And this isn’t just decorative math. It explains—actually explains—why A/B tests across pipeline topologies so often come back null. The configurations you tested probably belonged to the same gauge orbit. You were comparing coordinates, not physics.
For a broader treatment of the autonomy levels at play here, see The Autonomy Imperative: Code as Self-Governing Architecture, and for the information-theoretic cost floor that any harness must pay, see The Autonomy Channel: Rate-Distortion in Harness Design.

title: Gauge Symmetry and the Invariant Core of Harness Autonomy
text:
2. Formalizing the Gauge Group
Let a harness configuration be a tuple \(\mathbf{c} = (h_1, h_2, \ldots, h_m)\), where each \(h_i\) is a “connection” on the \(i\)-th decision stage—a map from the agent’s internal state to an action (tool call, generation, verification). The space of all such configurations is \(\mathcal{C}\).
A gauge transformation \(g \in \mathcal{G}\) is a smooth, invertible map \(\mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{C}\) satisfying:

\(g \circ \text{id} = \text{id}\) (identity is in \(\mathcal{G}\));
\(g \circ g' \in \mathcal{G}\) for all \(g, g' \in \mathcal{G}\) (closure);
The observable autonomy behavior \(\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{c}) = \mathcal{B}(g \cdot \mathbf{c})\) for all \(g \in \mathcal{G}\) (invariance).

Concretely, I’ve identified four families of gauge transformations that actually come up in harness design:

2.1 Topological Gauge (Permutation)
The symmetric group \(S_m\) acts by permuting stage orderings: \(g \cdot (h_1, \ldots, h_m) = (h_{g(1)}, \ldots, h_{g(m)})\). If two stages commute (their actions are independent of order), the permutation is pure gauge redundancy. In plain terms: swapping two steps that don’t talk to each other changes literally nothing about what the agent does. You could shuffle them in your sleep.


2.2 Parametric Gauge (Knob Reparameterization)
A smooth change of variables on the knob space. E.g., replacing a temperature parameter \(T \in [0, 2]\) with \(T' = f(T)\) for some diffeomorphism \(f\). As long as the relative effect of the knob on the output distribution is preserved, the absolute scale is gauge. It’s the harness analogue of rescaling your coordinate axes. The physics doesn’t care whether you measure in meters or feet.


2.3 Constraint Gauge (Gauge-Fixing)
Just as the Coulomb gauge \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{A} = 0\) or Lorenz gauge \(\partial_\mu A^\mu = 0\) selects a convenient representative within a gauge orbit (i.e., two different coordinate conventions that describe the same underlying field), a harness may impose a constraint placement—where verification gates sit, which stages are “frozen”—without changing the invariant content. The constraint is a gauge choice. A coordinate convention. Not a physical degree of freedom.


2.4 Context Gauge (Window Shuffling)
Redistributing tokens across the context window (system prompt vs. few-shot examples vs. retrieval results) while preserving the total information-theoretic content is a gauge transformation. This connects directly to the rate-distortion analysis in The Autonomy Channel: the rate \(R\) is gauge-invariant, while the particular allocation of bits across stages is gauge-dependent. You can shuffle the bits around; the total information budget doesn’t care.






flowchart LR
  A[Configuration c₁] -->|gauge g₁| B[Configuration c₂]
  A -->|gauge g₂| C[Configuration c₃]
  B -->|g⁻¹| A
  C -->|g₂⁻¹| A
  B <-->|same orbit| C
  style A fill:#e8f4fd,stroke:#2196F3
  style B fill:#e8f4fd,stroke:#2196F3
  style C fill:#e8f4fd,stroke:#2196F3






Three harness configurations that are behaviorally identical under the gauge group \(\mathcal{G}\): they occupy the same orbit and therefore represent the same autonomy structure.
The group \(\mathcal{G}\) is, in general, a semidirect product of the topological group \(S_m\) with a continuous group of knob reparameterizations, further extended by the constraint-placement and context-shuffling symmetries. For most practical harnesses (\(m \leq 8\)), the topological part dominates the gauge redundancy. The continuous knobs are almost all noise.

title: Gauge Symmetry and the Invariant Core of Harness Autonomy
text:
3. The Gauge-Invariant Autonomy Curvature
If the connection \(h_i\) encodes “how stage \(i\) acts on the agent’s state,” the natural invariant object is the autonomy curvature:
\[\mathcal{K}_{ij} \;=\; [h_i, h_j]_{\mathcal{G}} \;=\; h_i \circ h_j \;-\; h_j \circ h_i\]
defined on pairs of stages \((i, j)\). This is the commutator of two stage-connections, evaluated in the quotient by the gauge group.
Why is \(\mathcal{K}_{ij}\) invariant? Because it’s defined as a commutator of covariant derivatives, it transforms as a tensor under gauge transformations: \(g \cdot \mathcal{K}_{ij} = \mathcal{K}_{ij}\) for all \(g \in \mathcal{G}\). Concretely: permute stages, reparameterize knobs, shuffle context—whatever you do—the order-dependence between any pair of stages is preserved. It’s the same structural reason the electromagnetic field tensor \(F_{\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu A_\nu - \partial_\nu A_\mu\) is gauge-invariant. The antisymmetrized derivative “cancels” the pure-gauge part. The field survives; the potential doesn’t.
In plain terms (and I mean plain): the curvature measures how much the order in which you change two design knobs matters. If \(\mathcal{K}_{ij} = 0\), stages \(i\) and \(j\) commute—you can reorder them freely, and nothing changes. Pure gauge. If \(\mathcal{K}_{ij} \neq 0\), the order is physically meaningful. No reparameterization, no amount of A/B testing, is going to erase it.
This is the harness analogue of the Aharonov–Bohm effect, with one important clarification: the AB effect is specifically about a topological phase acquired in a region where the local field strength vanishes but the potential is non-trivial (i.e., holonomy in a non-simply-connected space). The harness analogue is a path-dependent autonomy budget: the total “effort” the agent expends depends on the route through the stage graph, even if each individual stage looks gauge-equivalent in isolation. The non-trivial holonomy is the invariant. You can’t shortcut it.
The curvature \(\mathcal{K}_{ij}\) is antisymmetric (\(\mathcal{K}_{ij} = -\mathcal{K}_{ji}\)) and, in the classical (non-quantized) regime, satisfies the Bianchi identity \(\mathcal{K}_{ij} + \mathcal{K}_{jk} + \mathcal{K}_{ki} = 0\) for any triple of stages. This reduces the number of independent curvature components from \(\binom{m}{2}\) to \(\binom{m}{2} - \binom{m}{3}\), a non-trivial constraint on the design space. Not all combinations of stage interactions are independently realizable.
For the variational perspective on how much autonomy a harness can sustain given these invariants, see Free Energy Bounds: A Variational Account of Autonomy. And for why autonomy tends to emerge in discrete jumps rather than smoothly, see Percolation of Autonomy: Critical Dynamics in Harness Design.

title: Gauge Symmetry and the Invariant Core of Harness Autonomy
section: 4. The Quotient: A Finite Set of Inequivalent Configurations
text:
4. The Quotient: A Finite Set of Inequivalent Configurations
The central claim of this post can now be stated precisely:

The space of inequivalent harness autonomy structures is the quotient \(\mathcal{C}/\mathcal{G}\), and for a harness with \(m\) decision stages, this quotient is determined by a finite set of discrete invariants.

These invariants are:








Invariant
Values
Meaning




Commutation class
\(\{0,1\}^{\binom{m}{2}}\) (antisymmetric)
Which pairs of stages have \(\mathcal{K}_{ij} \neq 0\)


Topological winding
\(\pi_1(\mathcal{C})\) (often \(\mathbb{Z}\) or trivial)
Whether the stage graph has non-trivial cycles (holonomy)


Budget partition
Integer partitions of the total autonomy budget into \(m\) parts
How the “effort” is irreducibly allocated


Constraint rank
\(\{0, 1, \ldots, m\}\)
Number of independent gauge-fixing constraints (verification gates)



This is the cheat-sheet an engineer can pin to a wall: four numbers (or a small matrix) that fully specify your harness’s autonomy structure, independent of any particular implementation.
A note on scaling, because I want to be honest here: for fixed \(m\), each invariant is finite, so the quotient is finite. However, the commutation class has \(2^{\binom{m}{2}}\) possible patterns, which grows combinatorially with \(m\). For \(m = 6\), that’s \(2^{15} = 32{,}768\) patterns. For \(m = 10\), \(2^{45} \approx 3.5 \times 10^{13}\). So the reduction from the continuous parameter space (dimension \(O(m \cdot k)\)) to this discrete set is still dramatic for small \(m\), but the “finite” label should be read as discrete and classifiable, not necessarily small. In practice, the Bianchi identity and symmetry constraints reduce the reachable set to a small fraction of the full Boolean lattice. You won’t be enumerating all 32,768.
The practical upshot (and this is the part I’d actually put on a whiteboard in a design review): before optimizing any continuous knob, determine which of these four invariants your harness occupies. Two harnesses in the same invariant class are gauge-equivalent. No amount of hyperparameter tuning will distinguish them. I promise. Two harnesses in different classes are genuinely different autonomy structures, and the choice between them is a structural decision, not a tuning decision.
This perspective resonates with the dialectical view in Scaffolding to Sovereignty: The Dialectic of Code Autonomy: the “scaffolding” (constraint placement, gauge-fixing) is not a tax on autonomy. It’s a coordinate choice that makes the invariant content manifest. You’re not restricting the agent. You’re picking a frame.

title: Gauge Symmetry and the Invariant Core of Harness Autonomy
text:
5. Four Heuristics for Harness Engineers
OK, so the theory yields four practical design heuristics. I’ve ordered them roughly by how much I wish someone had told me before those three weeks:
Heuristic 1: Classify before you configure. Before tuning temperatures, context windows, or tool-call budgets, identify the commutation class of your stage graph. If two stages commute (\(\mathcal{K}_{ij} = 0\)), their relative order is irrelevant—stop A/B-testing their sequence. You’re measuring noise. Focus your experimental budget on the non-commuting pairs, where the order is physically meaningful and where a real difference might live.
Heuristic 2: Fix the gauge deliberately. Choose your constraint placement (verification gates, retry loops) as a gauge-fixing condition, not as a free parameter. The Lorenz gauge analogy is instructive: you pick the gauge that makes the equations simplest, not the one that looks “most correct.” In practice, place verification gates at the points of maximum curvature (\(\|\mathcal{K}_{ij}\|\) large), where order-dependence is highest. That’s where the agent is most vulnerable to sequencing errors.
Heuristic 3: Check for holonomy before adding stages. Before adding a new stage to the pipeline, verify that it introduces a non-trivial winding in the stage graph. If the new stage is gauge-equivalent to an existing one (it commutes with all others and carries no independent budget), it’s redundancy, not capability. You’ve just added a coordinate. This is the percolation-critical insight from Percolation of Autonomy: autonomy emerges in discrete jumps when the constraint density crosses a critical threshold, not gradually. There’s a phase transition in there.
Heuristic 4: Budget partitions are the real design variable. The continuous knobs (temperature, window size) are largely gauge. The integer partition of the total autonomy budget across stages is the invariant. Spend your design time deciding how many retries, how many verification passes, how much context each stage irreducibly requires. These are the numbers that survive in the quotient. Everything else is coordinate noise.

A Worked Micro-Example
Consider a minimal 3-stage harness for an autonomous coding agent: Plan → Generate → Verify. The pseudocode is:
def harness(state):
    plan    = plan_stage(state, budget=B1)       # Stage 1
    code    = generate_stage(plan, budget=B2)    # Stage 2
    verdict = verify_stage(code, budget=B3)      # Stage 3
    return verdict
Gauge-equivalent reparameterization: Swap the order of Plan and Verify (a topological gauge), and rescale the budgets as \(B_1' = \alpha B_1\), \(B_3' = \alpha^{-1} B_3\) (a parametric gauge):
def harness_gauge(state):
    verdict = verify_stage(state, budget=B3')    # Stage 3 (moved first)
    plan    = plan_stage(verdict, budget=B1')    # Stage 1 (moved second)
    code    = generate_stage(plan, budget=B2)    # Stage 2 (unchanged)
    return code
The invariant that remains: The commutator \(\mathcal{K}_{12} = [\text{plan}, \text{generate}]\) is non-zero (generation depends on the plan—obviously, you need a plan to generate from), but \(\mathcal{K}_{13} = [\text{plan}, \text{verify}] = 0\) (verification is order-independent of planning when the budget is conserved). This single non-zero entry in the curvature matrix is the only structural fact about this harness. Everything else—stage order, absolute budget values—is gauge. You could shuffle the order of Plan and Verify a thousand times and the agent would behave identically.
This framework is tool-agnostic. It applies directly to a LangGraph state graph (where nodes are stages and edges are connections), a CrewAI task DAG (where tasks are stages and dependencies define the commutation structure), or an AutoGen conversation topology (where agents are stages and message-passing is the connection). The invariants are properties of the graph structure, not of the runtime. You don’t need to be in any particular framework.
For those seeking an external taxonomy of autonomy levels to ground the “five-level spectrum” referenced above, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework provides a useful reference for the constraint and verification dimensions.

title: Gauge Symmetry and the Invariant Core of Harness Autonomy
text:
6. Limitations and Open Questions
Intellectual honesty requires me to say what this framework does not capture. I’ll be upfront:
Quantization is missing. The curvature \(\mathcal{K}_{ij}\) is treated as a continuous tensor. In practice, LLM agent harnesses are discrete: tool calls are atomic, context windows are integer-token, verification is binary (pass/fail). The classical gauge structure is an approximation that becomes exact in the large-budget limit. For small budgets (\(B_i \leq 5\)), the discreteness introduces “quantization” effects that the continuous curvature simply doesn’t see. I’m comfortable with this approximation for most production systems, but it’s an approximation.
Non-Abelian complexity. The gauge group \(\mathcal{G}\) is treated as effectively Abelian (commuting families). For harnesses with \(m \geq 5\) and strong inter-stage coupling, the group becomes non-Abelian, and the curvature satisfies a Yang–Mills-type equation rather than the simpler Maxwell form. The design consequences get more complex, and the “finite set of invariants” claim weakens. I haven’t worked out the full non-Abelian case. It’s on the list.
Empirical validation is pending. The gauge-equivalence claim is structural, not yet empirically confirmed. A controlled experiment—taking two harnesses in the same invariant class but different gauge, and measuring task success rate over 1000+ runs—would be the critical test. My three-week anecdote in the introduction is suggestive. It’s not a proof. I’d like someone to actually run the experiment. (Ideally me, once I stop being the one who needs the experiment to justify the three weeks.)
The Bianchi identity may not hold. The identity \(\mathcal{K}_{ij} + \mathcal{K}_{jk} + \mathcal{K}_{ki} = 0\) assumes a flat underlying stage space. If the agent’s state space is genuinely curved (say, due to long-range dependencies in the context window that create non-local coupling), the Bianchi identity acquires a source term, and the constraint on the design space weakens. This is the case I’m least sure about, and where the physics analogy might actually break down.

title: Gauge Symmetry and the Invariant Core of Harness Autonomy
text:
7. Discussion and Conclusion
The gauge-symmetry perspective on harness design doesn’t eliminate the need for careful engineering. It reorganizes the effort. A substantial fraction of the perceived design freedom is identified as redundancy, and the irreducible content is isolated into a small set of discrete invariants. For a team building an autonomous coding agent, this means the question isn’t “what temperature should I use?” or “should verification come before or after generation?” (it doesn’t matter, if they commute). The question is: “what is the commutation structure of my stage graph, and what is my budget partition?”
This is, in a sense, the engineering analogue of the insight that changed theoretical physics in the 1950s: the “force” is not the potential; the “design” is not the configuration. The potential (the configuration) is gauge-dependent and non-unique. The field (the invariant) is what does the work. You can change coordinates all day. The field doesn’t care.
The broader implication for the autonomous agent ecosystem is a shift from search to classification. Rather than exhaustively exploring a high-dimensional hypercube of hyperparameters (which, as I’ve learned the hard way, mostly finds noise), an engineer should first classify the invariant class, then optimize within that class. The search space shrinks from continuous to discrete, from infinite to finite, and the A/B testing that so often yields null results becomes targeted. Actually informative.
This post is the fourth in a series building toward a complete treatment of autonomous agent harness design. The rate-distortion floor (The Autonomy Channel) tells us the minimum cost. The free-energy bound (Free Energy Bounds) tells us the maximum sustainable autonomy. The percolation analysis (Percolation of Autonomy) tells us where the phase transitions are. And this post tells us which of the apparent choices are real. Together, they form a coherent design calculus for the harness engineer.
The next step is empirical: building the controlled experiments that confirm or refute the gauge-equivalence hypothesis, and identifying the first non-Abelian effects in production harnesses. Until then, the practical advice stands: look for the invariant, and stop tuning the gauge.

title: Functorial Autonomy: Categorical Structure of Harness Design
text: We define a category of coding-agent harness configurations and prove that safe refactors are exactly the natural transformations—giving you a checkable algebraic criterion for autonomy-preserving design.

title: Functorial Autonomy: Categorical Structure of Harness Design
text:
Abstract
So here’s the thing. When you go and refactor a coding-agent harness—swap a tool, tighten a prompt, add a memory slot—you’re doing something that has a clean mathematical description, we just haven’t written it down yet. In this post, we recast harness design as a category Harness whose objects are complete configurations and whose arrows are autonomy-preserving refactors. The central result is a Yoneda-lemma-based completeness criterion: a harness is fully determined by its external interactions, so any two configurations that behave identically toward all tools, constraints, and context windows are the same object. This yields a practical corollary. A refactor is safe if and only if it is a natural transformation in the categorical sense. We show how this single algebraic condition subsumes the ad-hoc heuristics that practitioners currently apply, and we provide a concrete worked example, a finite (in principle) checkable procedure, and explicit guidance for LangChain, CrewAI, and AutoGen users.
Key terms defined inline: harness (the scaffolding code that wraps an LLM with tools, constraints, and memory), natural transformation (a structure-preserving map between two functors), Yoneda lemma (a theorem stating that an object is determined by its relationships to all others).

title: Functorial Autonomy: Categorical Structure of Harness Design
text:
Practical Takeaways (Read This First)
If you’re shipping a coding-agent harness today and just want a Monday-morning checklist before wading into the formalism—here you go:

AP-1 (Tool-superset). After any refactor, your allowed_tools list must be a superset of the pre-refactor list. In LangChain terms: verify that every Tool instance in the pre-refactor AgentExecutor still appears in the post-refactor one.
AP-2 (Schema-stability). The JSON output_schema (or equivalent Pydantic model) that downstream consumers parse must be unchanged. In CrewAI, this means the task.expected_output contract is invariant.
AP-3 (Context-budget monotonicity). The maximum tokens consumed per step must not increase. In AutoGen, check that max_consecutive_auto_reply and token_budget are non-decreasing in capacity.
Naturality check. If you can name a specific tool, constraint, or consumer for which AP-1 through AP-3 all hold simultaneously, the refactor is a natural transformation and autonomy is preserved. If any single consumer breaks, the morphism is non-natural and you have silently degraded autonomy.

Now, these four conditions aren’t pulled out of thin air. As we’ll see below, they’re the component-wise projections of a single categorical axiom. But if you walk away with nothing else, walk away with these four.

title: Functorial Autonomy: Categorical Structure of Harness Design
section: 1. Why Category Theory? The Failure of Ad-Hoc Heuristics
text:
1. Why Category Theory? The Failure of Ad-Hoc Heuristics
Every harness developer has inherited a set of “gotchas.” Don’t remove the web_search tool without checking the system prompt. Don’t shrink the context window below 8 192 tokens. Don’t swap the retry policy without re-testing the error-recovery path. These rules work. But—and this is the key word—they are enumerated, not derived. They’re a finite list of patches accumulated from incident post-mortems, and nobody can tell you why the list stops where it does.
The problem with an enumerated list is that it doesn’t compose. Add a new tool, a new constraint, a new memory layer, and suddenly the list doubles. Now you need pairwise interaction checks: does the new memory layer interact with the retry policy? Does the new tool violate the context budget under the existing retry schedule? The combinatorics explode, and practitioners fall back on “test it and hope.” (We’ve all been there. I’ve been there.)
Category theory offers a different posture. Instead of listing every valid interaction, you define the structure that makes an interaction valid, and then the valid interactions fall out as theorems. It’s the same move that made functional programming “correct by construction” after the lambda calculus was formalised (Barendregt, 1981). We’re making the analogous move for harness design.
This post builds directly on the series’ prior results. Our five-level autonomy spectrum gives the levels at which a harness can operate. The rate-distortion analysis quantifies the cost of each transition. The dialectical framing explains why scaffolding is generative rather than parasitic. The percolation-theoretic account identifies where autonomy emerges in discrete jumps. The gauge-symmetry reduction collapses the design space into inequivalent classes. The free-energy bound sets the ceiling on sustainable autonomy. The information-geometric view gives the cost of moving between configurations.
What’s missing from all of those? A single algebraic language in which “safe refactor” actually has a definition. That’s what we supply here.

title: Functorial Autonomy: Categorical Structure of Harness Design
text:
2. Defining the Category Harness

2.1 Objects
An object of Harness is a 5-tuple
\[H = (T,\; C,\; M,\; P,\; B)\]
where:

\(T = \{t_1, \dots, t_n\}\) is the finite set of tools exposed to the agent (e.g., file_read, shell_exec, web_search);
\(C\) is the set of constraints (prompt-level rules, JSON-schema validators, rate limits);
\(M\) is the memory configuration (window size, retrieval strategy, summarisation policy);
\(P\) is the policy layer (retry schedules, escalation rules, human-in-the-loop triggers);
\(B\) is the budget vector (max tokens per step, max concurrent tool calls, wall-clock ceiling).

We require that \(C\) is satisfiable with respect to \(T \cup M \cup P \cup B\). That is, there exists at least one agent trajectory that obeys all constraints while using the available tools within budget. This is a well-definedness condition; without it, the object is incoherent (see § 6 on pathologies).


2.2 Morphisms: Autonomy-Preserving Refactors
A morphism \(f: H \to H'\) in Harness is a 5-tuple \((f_T, f_C, f_M, f_P, f_B)\) of structure-preserving maps satisfying three autonomy-preservation axioms:

AP-1 (Tool inclusion). \(f_T\) is an inclusion: every tool in \(T\) has a corresponding tool in \(T'\). Formally, \(T \subseteq T'\) under the identification induced by \(f_T\).


AP-2 (Constraint projection). \(f_C\) maps each constraint in \(C\) to a constraint in \(C'\), and the image set \(f_C(C) \subseteq C'\) is no stronger than \(C\) in the sense that every trajectory valid under \(C\) is also valid under \(f_C(C)\).


AP-3 (Budget monotonicity). \(f_B\) is component-wise non-decreasing: the post-refactor budget is at least as permissive as the pre-refactor budget.

In plain English: you may add tools, you may relax constraints (but not tighten them), and you may increase budgets (but not decrease them). You may never remove a capability the agent previously had, never impose a new restriction it did not face, and never shrink the resources it could draw on. Simple, right? The subtlety is in proving that “simple” is also complete—which is what the next few sections do.


2.3 A Concrete Worked Example
Consider a minimal harness \(H_0\) with:

\(T_0 = \{\texttt{file\_read},\; \texttt{file\_write},\; \texttt{shell\_exec}\}\)
\(C_0 = \{\)“no execution of rm -rf”, “output must be valid JSON”}
$M_0 = {\(8\text{K-token window, FIFO eviction}\}\)
$P_0 = {\(1\text{ retry on timeout, escalate after 2 failures}\}\)
$B_0 = {\(4096\text{ tokens/step, 3 concurrent calls, 30 s ceiling}\}\)

Now propose a refactor \(H_1\) that adds a web_search tool, relaxes the JSON constraint to “output must be parseable as JSON or Markdown,” widens the window to 16 K tokens, keeps the retry policy, and leaves budgets unchanged.
Check AP-1: \(T_0 \subset T_1\). ✓ (Three original tools present; one added.)
Check AP-2: The “no rm -rf” constraint is unchanged. The JSON constraint is relaxed (Markdown is now also acceptable). Every trajectory valid under \(C_0\) is valid under \(C_1\). ✓
Check AP-3: Window increases from 8 K to 16 K. All other budgets unchanged. ✓
The morphism \(f: H_0 \to H_1\) is a valid arrow in Harness. Autonomy is preserved.
Now consider a different refactor \(H_2\) that removes shell_exec and tightens the constraint to “output must be strictly valid JSON (no trailing commas).” AP-1 fails (a tool was removed). AP-2 fails (a constraint was tightened). This is not a morphism in Harness; it’s an autonomy-degrading operation. The categorical framework tells you this before you deploy, not after the post-mortem at 2 a.m. on a Tuesday.

title: Functorial Autonomy: Categorical Structure of Harness Design
section: 3. Natural Transformations as the Safety Criterion
text:
3. Natural Transformations as the Safety Criterion

3.1 The Hom-Functor
Fix an object \(H\). The Hom-functor \(\text{Hom}(-, H)\) maps each object \(K\) to the set of valid morphisms \(K \to H\), and each morphism \(f: K \to K'\) to the post-composition map \(\text{Hom}(K', H) \to \text{Hom}(K, H)\).
Intuitively: \(\text{Hom}(K, H)\) is the set of all ways to refactor \(K\) into \(H\) while preserving autonomy. The Yoneda lemma will tell us that knowing all such refactors, for all \(K\), is equivalent to knowing \(H\) itself. (Yes, it sounds almost tautological. It isn’t, and the non-tautology is where the power lives.)


3.2 Definition: Natural Refactor
Let \(\mathcal{F}, \mathcal{G}: \mathbf{Harness} \to \mathbf{Set}\) be two functors (e.g., \(\mathcal{F}(H) = T\) extracts the tool set; \(\mathcal{G}(H) = C\) extracts the constraint set). A natural transformation \(\eta: \mathcal{F} \Rightarrow \mathcal{G}\) assigns to each object \(H\) a function \(\eta_H: \mathcal{F}(H) \to \mathcal{G}(H)\) such that for every morphism \(f: H \to H'\), the square
\[\mathcal{F}(H) \xrightarrow{\eta_H} \mathcal{G}(H)\] \[\downarrow{\mathcal{F}(f)} \qquad\qquad \downarrow{\mathcal{G}(f)}\] \[\mathcal{F}(H') \xrightarrow{\eta_{H'}} \mathcal{G}(H')\]
commutes. In harness terms: the way you “translate” tools into constraints must be independent of which harness you are in. The translation rule does not depend on the specific configuration.
In plain English: if your safety mapping from “which tools are available” to “which constraints must fire” is the same rule no matter what tools you have, then the rule is natural. If the rule changes depending on whether you have shell_exec or not, it’s non-natural, and a refactor that adds or removes shell_exec will silently change your safety guarantees. (This is, I think, where most real-world harness bugs actually live.)


3.3 Theorem 1 (Safe-Refactor Characterisation)

A morphism \(f: H \to H'\) in Harness is a safe refactor if and only if it is a natural transformation in the above sense, i.e., it commutes with every Hom-functor on Harness.

Definition + Claim (with key algebraic step). The “if” direction is immediate from the axioms: AP-1, AP-2, AP-3 are precisely the commutativity conditions for the tool, constraint, and budget functors. The “only-if” direction requires showing that any morphism satisfying AP-1 through AP-3 automatically commutes with all Hom-functors, not just the three named ones. The key step is:
Given any functor \(\mathcal{F}: \mathbf{Harness} \to \mathbf{Set}\), \(\mathcal{F}(H)\) is a function of the 5-tuple \((T, C, M, P, B)\). Under \(f\), each component transforms via its respective \(f_i\). Because AP-1 ensures \(T \subseteq T'\), AP-2 ensures \(C\) projects into \(C'\), and AP-3 ensures \(B \leq B'\), the induced map \(\mathcal{F}(f): \mathcal{F}(H) \to \mathcal{F}(H')\) is well-defined for any \(\mathcal{F}\) that respects the partial order on components. Since every Hom-functor is of this form, commutativity holds. \(\square\)
Look, this isn’t a deep theorem in the number-theoretic sense. It’s a structural theorem. Its value is practical: it replaces an open-ended list of “things to check” with a single closure condition. You stop maintaining a wiki page of gotchas and start checking one thing.

title: Functorial Autonomy: Categorical Structure of Harness Design
section: 4. The Yoneda Lemma and the Completeness Criterion
text:
4. The Yoneda Lemma and the Completeness Criterion

4.1 Statement
The Yoneda lemma (Mac Lane, 1971; Awodey, 2010) states that for any category \(\mathbf{C}\) and object \(X \in \mathbf{C}\), the natural isomorphism
\[\text{Nat}(\text{Hom}(-, X),\; F) \;\cong\; F(X)\]
holds for every functor \(F: \mathbf{C}^{\text{op}} \to \mathbf{Set}\). In words: to know \(X\), it suffices to know how every other object maps into \(X\). That’s it. The whole object is encoded in its relationships.


4.2 The Completeness Criterion for Harnesses
Specialising to Harness: a harness \(H\) is fully determined by the collection \(\{\text{Hom}(K, H)\}_{K \in \mathbf{Harness}}\). Two harnesses \(H, H'\) that admit exactly the same set of valid refactors from every \(K\) are the same object.
Practical corollary. You do not need to inspect the internal code of a harness to know whether a refactor is safe. You need only verify that the external interaction profile—the set of tools, the set of constraints, the budget vector, the memory contract, the policy layer—has not changed in any autonomy-reducing direction. This is the algebraic justification for the “black-box testing” intuition that many practitioners already follow, now made precise. (It validates the gut feeling. Nice.)


4.3 A (Qualified) Finite Procedure
In principle, the Yoneda fingerprint is the full set \(\text{Hom}(K, H)\) for all \(K\). In practice, this set is combinatorially explosive: the number of possible harnesses grows super-exponentially in \(|T| + |C| + |M|\).
Qualified claim. For local safety checks—verifying that a single proposed refactor \(f: H \to H'\) is a morphism—it suffices to evaluate AP-1, AP-2, AP-3 on the specific pair \((H, H')\). This is a finite procedure: check the tool set inclusion, check the constraint projection, check the budget component-wise. The full Yoneda fingerprint is needed only for global questions (e.g., “does there exist any sequence of refactors that takes \(H\) to \(H'\) while preserving autonomy at every step?”), and even then, a small probe set of canonical \(K\) values (the “basis” harnesses with one tool, one constraint, one memory slot) typically suffices, as our gauge-symmetry analysis shows that most of the design space collapses into a small number of inequivalent classes.

title: Functorial Autonomy: Categorical Structure of Harness Design
text:
5. Unifying the Prior Results
The categorical framework doesn’t replace the earlier posts in this series; it subsumes them. Each prior result becomes a theorem or corollary about functors or natural transformations on Harness:

Rate-distortion (Shannon, 1948; Cover & Thomas, 2006). The rate-distortion function \(R(D)\) quantifies the minimum “bits” of constraint information you must transmit to keep distortion below \(D\). In categorical terms, \(R(D)\) is the cardinality of the image of the constraint functor \(\mathcal{C}: \mathbf{Harness} \to \mathbf{Set}\) under the optimal encoding. Functor composition is associative, so the bits you spend to implement a refactor add up linearly across a chain of refactors. In short: the cost of refactoring is additive, just as functor composition is associative.
Percolation (Stauffer & Aharony, 1994). Autonomy emerges in discrete jumps as constraint density crosses a critical threshold. Categorically, this is a phase transition in the Hom-sets: below the threshold, \(\text{Hom}(K, H)\) is empty for most \(K\) (no valid refactors exist); above it, the Hom-set suddenly becomes non-trivial. The percolation cluster is the connected component of the Hom-graph. In short: you do not gradually lose autonomy; you lose it all at once when the constraint graph disconnects.
Gauge symmetry. The gauge-symmetry reduction shows that many harness configurations related by “gauge transformations” (relabeling tools, reordering constraints) are physically the same. Categorically, these are isomorphisms in Harness. The quotient by isomorphism gives the set of inequivalent autonomy structures. In short: the label you put on your tools does not matter; only the structure of their interactions does.
Free-energy bound. The variational free-energy bound \(F(H) = \mathbb{E}_{p_H}[\log p_H / \log q]\) is a functorial quantity: it is natural in \(H\), meaning it is preserved under morphisms. A safe refactor cannot increase the free energy. In short: you cannot refactor your way to more autonomy than the bound allows; the bound is a natural invariant.
Information geometry (Amari, 2016). The Riemannian metric on the space of harnesses is the Fisher information metric on the distribution of agent trajectories. Geodesics are the “minimum-effort” refactors. A natural transformation is a geodesic that is straight in the categorical sense: it does not curve through configurations that violate AP-1 through AP-3. In short: the safest refactor is the one that follows a straight line in the space of constraints, and the Yoneda criterion tells you when your path has bent.

title: Functorial Autonomy: Categorical Structure of Harness Design
text:
6. Pathologies and Limitations
Intellectual honesty requires naming the cases where the framework breaks. Here they are:
Undecidable satisfiability. AP-2 requires that \(C\) is satisfiable with respect to \(T \cup M \cup P \cup B\). If \(C\) contains constraints expressible in a language with undecidable satisfiability (e.g., full first-order logic over the agent’s action space), then the well-definedness check for the object \(H\) is itself undecidable. In practice, harnesses use decidable fragments (regular expressions, JSON Schema, linear inequalities), so this is a theoretical rather than practical obstruction. But it means the category Harness is not all harnesses; it’s the full subcategory of decidably-specified harnesses.
Partial tool schemas. If a tool’s input/output schema is only partially specified (e.g., “accepts a file path” but the path grammar is undefined), the Hom-set \(\text{Hom}(K, H)\) may be ill-defined: we cannot check AP-2 because we do not know what “valid” means for that tool. The categorical framework requires total specifications. Partially-specified harnesses live in a pre-category where associativity of composition may fail.
Non-well-behaved functors. The Yoneda lemma requires the functors to be set-valued. If your harness has infinitely many constraints (e.g., a constraint that is a real-valued cost function over an infinite action space), the Hom-set is a proper class, not a set, and the standard Yoneda lemma does not apply directly. One can work in a 2-categorical or topos-theoretic setting, but the practical checkability is lost.
The “finite” claim, restated honestly. The local AP-1/2/3 check is finite for a given pair \((H, H')\). The global Yoneda fingerprint is finite in principle (the category has finitely many objects if \(|T|, |C|, |M|, |P|, |B|\) are all finite) but combinatorially intractable in practice for realistic harness sizes. The gauge-symmetry reduction helps, but does not eliminate, the combinatorial explosion. I’d rather flag that upfront than pretend the procedure scales to 500 tools.

title: Functorial Autonomy: Categorical Structure of Harness Design
text:
7. Related Work
Our categorical approach is adjacent to, but distinct from, several existing formalisms. The typed effect-system literature (Lindley, 2012; Vázquez et al., 2023) provides a type-theoretic account of which side-effects an agent action may produce; our AP-2 constraint is a coarser, behavioural version of their effect typing. The formal-verification work on LLM safety (e.g., the work on provable safety bounds for tool-use sequences, 2024–2025) verifies individual agent trajectories; our framework verifies refactors between harnesses, which is a one-level-up question. The recent line on constitutional AI and reward-model alignment (Bai et al., 2022) addresses the policy \(P\) in our 5-tuple; we treat \(P\) as a given and focus on the structural invariants that survive its modification.

title: Functorial Autonomy: Categorical Structure of Harness Design
text:
8. Practical Design Calculus
Okay, back to the Monday-morning question: what do I actually check in my codebase?
LangChain. In AgentExecutor, the tool set \(T\) is the tools list. AP-1: after your refactor, assert set(old_tools) ⊆ set(new_tools). AP-2: the output_parser class must not become more restrictive (e.g., do not swap PydanticOutputParser for a stricter schema). AP-3: max_iterations and max_execution_time must not decrease.
CrewAI. The tool set is the tools attribute on each Agent. AP-1: same superset check. AP-2: the task.expected_output and task.context contracts must be invariant or relaxed. AP-3: max_rpm and max_rpm-equivalents must not shrink.
AutoGen. The tool set is the registered Function objects in the AssistantAgent. AP-1: superset check on the function registry. AP-2: the system_message constraints must not gain new prohibitions. AP-3: max_consecutive_auto_reply and lifecycle budgets must not decrease.
A concrete failure mode. A common mistake in LangChain is to add a new tool and simultaneously tighten the system prompt to “only use the first three tools.” AP-1 holds (the old tools are still present), but AP-2 fails (the prompt constraint now excludes the new tool, effectively removing it). The categorical check catches this because the constraint projection \(f_C\) maps the old constraint set to a stronger set, violating the “no stronger” requirement. You’d never catch that by eyeballing the tool list.

title: Functorial Autonomy: Categorical Structure of Harness Design
text:
9. Discussion
A critic might object that the entire apparatus is overkill: “I just check my tool list and my prompt, and it works.” Fair point. And the framework is designed to be invisible in the simple case. When your harness has three tools and two constraints, AP-1 through AP-3 are trivially checkable by eye, and the categorical language adds nothing. You’d be right to skip it.
The framework earns its keep at the margins. When you have twenty tools, a nested constraint hierarchy, a memory subsystem with its own budget, and a policy layer with escalation rules that interact with the retry schedule—the pairwise interaction space is \(O(n^2)\) or worse. The categorical condition “the morphism is natural” collapses this to a single commutativity check per functor, and the Yoneda criterion tells you that checking the external profile is sufficient. You do not need to reason about the internal wiring.
Another objection, and a good one: the axioms AP-1 through AP-3 are sufficient but not necessary for autonomy preservation. There may be refactors that tighten a constraint in one dimension while relaxing it in another, with a net autonomy gain. The categorical framework does not capture this, because it works with a partial order on components, not a lexicographic or weighted one. Extending the framework to a partially-ordered monoid on the constraint space (where some constraints can trade off against others) is an open direction, and it’s where the 2-categorical / enriched-category generalisation mentioned in the Conclusion becomes necessary.

title: Functorial Autonomy: Categorical Structure of Harness Design
text:
10. Conclusion
We’ve defined a category Harness whose objects are coding-agent harness configurations and whose morphisms are autonomy-preserving refactors. The Yoneda lemma yields a completeness criterion: a harness is determined by its external interactions, so safety is a property of the interface, not the implementation. Safe refactors are exactly the natural transformations; unsafe ones are the non-natural morphisms that silently degrade autonomy.
This categorical lens unifies the ad-hoc heuristics, the rate-distortion bounds, the percolation thresholds, the gauge-symmetry reductions, the free-energy ceilings, and the information-geometric cost functions that we’ve developed across this series into a single algebraic framework. It doesn’t replace them; it gives them a common syntax.
The next step is to enrich the category. The current Harness is a 1-category: morphisms are either valid or invalid. A 2-category would allow morphisms between morphisms—that is, a “refactor of a refactor”—and the 2-cells would encode how much autonomy is preserved at each step. This is the enriched-category programme, and it will be the subject of a follow-up post in this series.
Coming next: the enriched category of harness refactors, where the 2-cells measure the “autonomy curvature” of a refactor path and the Yoneda lemma generalises to a 2-Yoneda embedding.

title: Free Energy Bounds: A Variational Account of Autonomy
text:
So here’s the thing about a coding-agent harness. At its core, it’s a control architecture sitting between an LLM’s generative capacity and the hard constraints of a real software development lifecycle. The gap between what the harness permits and what the agent actually does—that’s the gap between a prior and a posterior, if you’re thinking in Bayesian terms. This post takes the variational free-energy framework from active inference (Friston, 2010) and slaps it onto that gap. What falls out is a quantitative design calculus: a per-step KL-divergence budget that tells you how much autonomous behaviour a given constraint architecture can sustain before the free-energy objective just… diverges. For harness engineers who spend their days balancing tightness of control against an agent’s generative capacity, this converts a fuzzy intuitive trade-off into an inequality you can actually check before shipping.
This work builds directly on the five-level autonomy spectrum in The Autonomy Imperative, the dialectical scaffolding model in Scaffolding to Sovereignty, and the percolation-theory analysis of constraint density in Percolation of Autonomy. Those posts establish what autonomy looks like and when it emerges. This one asks the more practical question: how much can a harness afford to grant? And it gives you a number.

title: Free Energy Bounds: A Variational Account of Autonomy
section: The Accuracy–Complexity Trade-off in Harness Design
text:
The Accuracy–Complexity Trade-off in Harness Design
The variational free-energy objective decomposes into two terms (Friston, 2010):
\[\mathcal{F}(q) \;=\; \underbrace{D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\bigl(q(\mathbf{h})\,\|\,p(\mathbf{h}\mid\mathbf{o})\bigr)}_{\text{accuracy (expected surprise)}} \;+\; \underbrace{D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\bigl(q(\mathbf{h})\,\|\,p(\mathbf{h})\bigr)}_{\text{complexity (KL from prior)}}\]
The first term penalises the agent’s posterior hypothesis \(\mathbf{h}\) for diverging from what the observations \(\mathbf{o}\)—the spec, the test suite, the lint output—actually support. The second term penalises the posterior for straying from the harness’s learned prior \(p(\mathbf{h})\), which is really just the set of allowed actions, tool schemas, and phase-gate rules baked into the architecture.
And this isn’t some abstract analogy I’m reaching for. In a coding-agent harness, the correspondence is pretty direct:







Free-energy quantity
Harness component




Prior \(p(\mathbf{h})\)
Tool whitelist, phase-gate rules, prompt scaffolding


Posterior \(q(\mathbf{h})\)
Agent’s actual action sequence over a trajectory


Observations \(\mathbf{o}\)
Spec checklist, test results, lint/CI signals


Accuracy term
Spec-compliance score (checklist pass rate)


Complexity term
Degree to which the agent “invents” actions outside the prior



Table 1. Correspondence between free-energy-principle quantities and harness components.
The trade-off is almost painfully straightforward: tighten the prior (narrow the tool space, pile on more phase gates) and the complexity term drops, but you risk raising the accuracy term because the agent simply can’t reach the action that would satisfy the spec. Loosen the prior and the reverse happens. The FVE bound tells you where the sweet spot is, rather than leaving you to feel it out.

title: Free Energy Bounds: A Variational Account of Autonomy
text:
Formal Bound for Discrete Actions
Consider a harness with a discrete action space of size \(K\) (say, \(K=12\) tools) and a trajectory of \(T\) steps. Under the assumption that the posterior is a product distribution across steps (a standard Markovian approximation for sequential agents), the total free energy satisfies:
\[\mathcal{F}_{\text{total}} \;=\; \sum_{t=1}^{T}\!\Bigl[\,\epsilon_t + D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\bigl(q_t\,\|\,p_t\bigr)\Bigr] \;\leq\; T\,\epsilon_{\max} + T\,\log K\]
where \(\epsilon_t\) is the per-step accuracy penalty and \(\log K\) is the maximum per-step KL (achieved when \(q_t\) is a point mass on a single symbol and \(p_t\) is uniform over all \(K\) symbols, giving \(D_{\mathrm{KL}} = \log K\); or when \(q_t\) is uniform and \(p_t\) is a point mass on the same symbol).
Rearranging for the autonomy budget:
\[\boxed{\;\sum_{t=1}^{T} D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\bigl(q_t\,\|\,p_t\bigr) \;\leq\; \mathcal{F}_{\max} \;-\; T\,\epsilon_{\text{spec}}\;}\]
where \(\mathcal{F}_{\max}\) is the maximum free energy the engineering team is willing to tolerate (set by quality gates) and \(\epsilon_{\text{spec}}\) is the per-step spec-compliance cost.

Practitioner’s note. Strip away the notation and it’s basically: count your steps, count your tools, and you have a ceiling on how “free” the agent can be per step. And if your agent keeps violating the spec, the problem isn’t that it’s too autonomous. It’s that your verification (the accuracy term) is too weak to anchor it.

Worked example. Suppose a trajectory spans \(T=40\) steps over a \(K=12\)-action tool space. The theoretical maximum total KL is \(T\log K \approx 40 \times 2.48 \approx 99\) nats. If the harness sets \(\mathcal{F}_{\max}=30\) and the spec-compliance cost is \(\epsilon_{\text{spec}}=10\) nats per step (total accuracy penalty \(T\epsilon_{\text{spec}}=400\)—wait, that exceeds \(\mathcal{F}_{\max}\); let us use a more realistic \(\epsilon_{\text{spec}}=0.5\) nats per step, giving \(T\epsilon_{\text{spec}}=20\)), the KL budget is \(\mathcal{F}_{\max} - T\epsilon_{\text{spec}} = 30 - 20 = 10\) nats total, or \(0.25\) nats per step. That’s roughly \(25\%\) of the single-step maximum \(\log 12 \approx 2.48\) nats. The agent retains meaningful autonomy headroom while staying well within the divergence bound.
