title: Canalized Autonomy: Waddington Landscapes in Harness Design
text: So here’s the question that keeps coming up in harness design: how many constraints do I actually need to keep the agent productive without over-determining it? We recast this as a geometry problem on a Waddington epigenetic landscape, derive a computable canalization depth metric δ, and present a neutral-network traversal algorithm that safely removes constraints while preserving basin integrity. The framework applies directly to any LLM agent scaffold under active development.

title: Canalized Autonomy: Waddington Landscapes in Harness Design
text: So here’s the question that keeps coming up in harness design: how many constraints do I actually need to keep the agent productive without over-determining it? We recast this as a geometry problem on a Waddington epigenetic landscape, derive a computable canalization depth metric δ, and present a neutral-network traversal algorithm that safely removes constraints while preserving basin integrity. The framework applies directly to any LLM agent scaffold under active development.

title: Canalized Autonomy: Waddington Landscapes in Harness Design
text:
Key Takeaways

Canalization depth δ is a single scalar summarising how robustly a harness channels agent behaviour toward productive outputs, independent of the agent’s specific trajectory.
Complete autonomy (no hard constraints) corresponds to a landscape with a single global attractor basin; its geometry is computable from the harness specification alone.
Neutral-network traversal gives a step-by-step algorithm for removing one constraint at a time, with a verifiable invariant that the agent’s effective autonomy does not decrease.
The metric and algorithm are implementable today via constraint-satisfaction solvers (Z3, OR-Tools) and fit naturally into CI pipelines.
The framework unifies and contextualises the rate-distortion, spectral, percolation, and information-geometric results developed earlier in this series.

title: Canalized Autonomy: Waddington Landscapes in Harness Design
section: Where This Fits in the Series
text:
Where This Fits in the Series
This post is the geometric backbone of the harness-design series. Earlier entries establish what autonomy is (the five-level spectrum), how much information must flow through the harness (rate-distortion), and how fast it converges (spectral gap). Here we ask what shape the constraint space must have so that autonomy is robust rather than brittle. If you’re reading this in isolation, the only prerequisite is a working intuition that a “harness” is the set of prompts, tool-whitelists, output schemas, and retry policies that surround an LLM.

title: Canalized Autonomy: Waddington Landscapes in Harness Design
section: 1. The Intuition: A Valley, Not a Fence
text:
1. The Intuition: A Valley, Not a Fence
Waddington’s 1942 epigenetic landscape (Waddington, 1942) depicts cellular differentiation as a ball rolling down a crinkled surface: the folds are developmental constraints, the valleys are attractor states, and the ball’s final position is determined jointly by the terrain and the initial push. The crucial observation is that the ball does not need to be told where to go; the shape of the landscape does the steering.
A coding-agent harness is, in structural analogy, the terrain. The agent is the ball. The constraints—tool-whitelists, output-schema validators, retry budgets, permission gates—are the folds in the surface. A well-designed harness is not a cage; it’s a valley that guides the ball toward productive basins while leaving lateral freedom within the valley floor.

In plain terms: You don’t need to micromanage every function call. You need to shape the “ground” so that the agent’s natural momentum carries it toward correct outputs, and the sides of the valley prevent catastrophic deviations.

Now, this intuition isn’t exactly new. The dialectical framing establishes that scaffolding is the generative precondition of autonomy, not its tax. The percolation analysis shows that autonomy emerges in discrete jumps as constraint density crosses a critical threshold. What’s missing—and what this post is actually about—is a geometric account of how deep the valleys are and how to safely smooth them.

title: Canalized Autonomy: Waddington Landscapes in Harness Design
section: 2. Formal Setup: The Harness as a Landscape
text:
2. Formal Setup: The Harness as a Landscape
Okay, so we’ve got the picture. Now let’s fix notation so the geometric objects are actually precise.
Let \(\Sigma\) be the finite set of hard constraints in a harness specification (tool-whitelists, schema validators, permission gates, retry caps, etc.). For a constraint \(c \in \Sigma\), let \(\Phi_c : \mathcal{A} \to [0,1]\) be a restriction functional measuring the fraction of the agent’s action space \(\mathcal{A}\) that \(c\) eliminates. The harness potential is
\[\Phi_\sigma(\mathbf{a}) \;=\; \sum_{c \in \sigma} \Phi_c(\mathbf{a}), \qquad \sigma \subseteq \Sigma.\]
The Waddington landscape associated with \(\sigma\) is the pair \((\mathcal{A},\, \Phi_\sigma)\), where \(\mathcal{A}\) is (for analytical convenience) a compact Riemannian manifold with boundary, and \(\Phi_\sigma\) is a smooth, non-negative function whose zero set \(\mathcal{Z}_\sigma = \{\mathbf{a} : \Phi_\sigma(\mathbf{a})=0\}\) is the set of permitted agent states.

Remark (Why a manifold?). In practice \(\mathcal{A}\) is discrete (a finite set of tool calls, API endpoints, file paths). We embed it in a smooth manifold to access differential-geometric machinery—Hessian eigenvalues, basin volumes, curvature—without loss of fidelity. The embedding is via the information-geometric lift described in a companion post; the resulting metric tensor \(G\) is computable from the harness specification.


In plain terms: \(\Phi_\sigma\) is a “penalty score” for every possible agent action. Zero means “allowed”; large means “blocked.” The shape of this penalty surface is the harness.

Agent dynamics under the landscape are modelled by the overdamped Langevin SDE
\[d\mathbf{a}_t = -\nabla\Phi_\sigma(\mathbf{a}_t)\,dt + \sqrt{2\kappa}\,d\mathbf{W}_t,\]
where \(\kappa > 0\) is an effective “temperature” capturing the agent’s stochasticity (sampling randomness, context-window noise) and \(\mathbf{W}_t\) is standard Brownian motion on \(\mathcal{A}\).

In plain terms: The agent drifts downhill (toward low-penalty actions) while being kicked around by noise. The depth of the valley determines how far the noise can push it before it escapes.

title: Canalized Autonomy: Waddington Landscapes in Harness Design
text:
3. The Complete-Autonomy Limit
What about the extreme case \(\sigma = \varnothing\) (no hard constraints)? You get \(\Phi_\varnothing \equiv 0\): a flat landscape. And that’s not the autonomy we want—unconstrained drift is undirected. The meaningful complete-autonomy regime is \(\sigma = \{c_{\min}\}\), a single soft constraint (e.g., “produce valid JSON”) that defines a unique global minimum \(\mathbf{a}^*\).
Proposition 1 (Single-basin geometry). If \(\Phi_{\{c_{\min}\}}\) is strictly convex on \(\mathcal{A}\), the landscape possesses exactly one attractor basin \(\mathcal{B}^*\), and the basin volume \(\text{Vol}(\mathcal{B}^*)\) is computable from the Hessian \(\nabla^2\Phi_{c_{\min}}(\mathbf{a}^*)\) via the Gaussian approximation
\[\text{Vol}(\mathcal{B}^*) \;\approx\; (2\pi)^{d/2}\,|\nabla^2\Phi(\mathbf{a}^*)|^{-1/2}.\]

In plain terms: If the “valley” has a single, well-defined bottom and the sides are monotonically rising, there’s exactly one place the ball ends up, and we can calculate how wide the valley is from the curvature at the bottom.

This is the geometric content of the free-energy bound: the basin volume is the agent’s effective autonomy, and the Hessian determinant encodes the structural cost floor identified in the rate-distortion analysis.

title: Canalized Autonomy: Waddington Landscapes in Harness Design
text:
4. Canalization Depth: A Robustness Metric
Here’s the central contribution: the canalization depth \(\delta(\sigma)\), defined as the minimum “energy barrier” an agent must surmount to escape the productive basin \(\mathcal{B}^*\):
\[\delta(\sigma) \;=\; \min_{\mathbf{a} \in \partial\mathcal{B}^*} \;\Phi_\sigma(\mathbf{a}) \;-\; \min_{\mathbf{b} \in \mathcal{B}^*}\;\Phi_\sigma(\mathbf{b}).\]
Equivalently, \(\delta\) is the depth of the valley measured from rim to floor.

In plain terms: \(\delta\) answers the question “how hard is it for the agent to accidentally do something outside the productive range?” A large \(\delta\) means the valley is deep—robust. A small \(\delta\) means the agent is one noisy step from escaping into unproductive territory.

Properties.

Monotonicity: If \(\sigma' \supseteq \sigma\), then \(\delta(\sigma') \geq \delta(\sigma)\). Adding constraints can only deepen the valley.
Computability: For piecewise-quadratic \(\Phi_\sigma\) (the common case when constraints are linear-inequality or box constraints), \(\delta\) reduces to a linear programme over the constraint normals. For general \(\Phi_\sigma\), it’s a convex optimisation problem solvable to any \(\epsilon\) in polynomial time (assuming the landscape is a convex function on \(\mathcal{A}\), which holds for the standard constraint families).
Invariance: \(\delta\) is invariant under the gauge transformations that reparameterise the harness without changing the induced agent dynamics. Thus \(\delta\) is a genuine invariant of the autonomy structure, not an artefact of a particular encoding.


In plain terms: You can rephrase your constraints, rename your tools, reformat your prompts—as long as the effective restriction on the agent’s action space is the same, \(\delta\) does not change. It measures the geometry, not the syntax.

title: Canalized Autonomy: Waddington Landscapes in Harness Design
section: 5. Neutral-Network Traversal: Safely Simplifying the Harness
text:
5. Neutral-Network Traversal: Safely Simplifying the Harness
So the practical question every harness designer eventually hits is: which constraint can I actually remove without letting the agent escape the basin? This is exactly the neutral-network problem from evolutionary biology (Kauffman & Levin, 1987; Kauffman, 1993): a neutral step is a mutation that changes the genotype (here, the constraint set) without changing the phenotype (here, the basin \(\mathcal{B}^*\) and the canalization depth \(\delta\)).
Definition. A constraint \(c \in \sigma\) is neutral with respect to \(\sigma\) if
\[\mathcal{B}^*(\sigma \setminus \{c\}) = \mathcal{B}^*(\sigma) \quad\text{and}\quad \delta(\sigma \setminus \{c\}) \geq \delta(\sigma) - \varepsilon,\]
for a designer-specified tolerance \(\varepsilon > 0\).

5.1 Traversal Algorithm






flowchart TD
  A[Start: harness σ, tolerance ε] --> B{Enumerate constraints c ∈ σ}
  B --> C[Compute δ(σ \ {c})]
  C --> D{δ(σ \ {c}) ≥ δ(σ) − ε AND basin unchanged?}
  D -- Yes --> E[Commit removal: σ ← σ \ {c}]
  D -- No --> F[Reject: keep c]
  E --> G{More constraints to test?}
  F --> G
  G -- Yes --> B
  G -- No --> H[Output: simplified harness σ*]






Each “Reject” branch preserves the current harness; the algorithm only commits when both invariants (basin identity and depth tolerance) hold. The procedure terminates because \(\Sigma\) is finite.
Correctness sketch. By induction on \(|\sigma|\): the base case \(|\sigma|=1\) is the single-basin proposition. The inductive step relies on the fact that removing a neutral constraint is a natural transformation in the category of harnesses—i.e., it preserves all autonomy invariants simultaneously.


5.2 Worked Example (Three Constraints)
Suppose the harness \(\sigma = \{c_1, c_2, c_3\}\) contains:








Constraint
Type
Effect




\(c_1\): tool-whitelist
Hard
Agent may only call read_file, write_file, run_test


\(c_2\): output-schema
Hard
Final response must be valid JSON matching schema \(S\)


\(c_3\): retry-budget
Soft
At most 3 tool-call retries per task



Measured values: \(\delta(\sigma) = 0.72\) (arbitrary normalisation).
Step 1. Test \(c_3\). Remove it: \(\delta(\sigma\setminus\{c_3\}) = 0.71\). Basin unchanged. \(0.71 \geq 0.72 - 0.05\). Neutral → commit.
Step 2. Test \(c_2\). Remove it: \(\delta(\sigma\setminus\{c_2\}) = 0.34\). Basin fragments (agent may now emit free text). Reject → keep \(c_2\).
Step 3. Test \(c_1\). Remove it: \(\delta\) drops to 0.11; basin vanishes. Reject → keep \(c_1\).
Result: \(\sigma^* = \{c_1, c_2\}\). The retry budget was redundant; the other two constraints are load-bearing. The agent retains full lateral freedom within the JSON-producing, whitelisted-tool basin.

In plain terms: You tried removing each constraint one at a time. The retry limit turned out to be decorative—the agent was already well-behaved without it. The tool whitelist and the output schema, however, are structural: remove either, and the agent’s behaviour scatters.



5.3 Implementation Note
In practice, you encode \(\Phi_\sigma\) as a constraint-satisfaction problem in Z3 or OR-Tools and compute \(\delta\) via a sequence of linear programmes (one per constraint boundary facet). The neutral-test loop is a simple for-over-constraints with a solver call per iteration. A reference implementation for the three-constraint example above is ~40 lines of Python and fits in a CI job that runs on every harness-spec change. This connects directly to the CI-auditable refactoring plan derived in the Wasserstein companion.

title: Canalized Autonomy: Waddington Landscapes in Harness Design
text:
6. Practical Considerations and Limitations


Click to expand caveats and edge cases

The ball is not point-like. The Langevin model treats the agent as a single state vector. A real LLM agent has a context window, a tool-call history, and a multi-step plan. These are higher-order state variables that the one-dimensional landscape does not capture. The RG-flow analysis provides the coarse-graining prescription: integrate out fast variables (individual tokens) to obtain an effective landscape on the slow manifold (task-level decisions). The \(\delta\) computed on the coarse-grained landscape is the one that matters for design.
Strict convexity is a modelling assumption. Real harnesses often produce non-convex \(\Phi_\sigma\) (e.g., “either use the REST API or the gRPC API, but not both” creates a disconnected feasible set). In that case \(\delta\) becomes a minimum over multiple basins, and the neutral-network algorithm must be run per-basin. The cohomological obstruction theorem characterises when such disconnectedness is topologically unavoidable versus a parametric artefact.
Temperature \(\kappa\) is agent-specific. The same harness yields different \(\delta\)-effective values for different LLMs (different sampling temperatures, different context-lengths, different instruction-following fidelity). The \(\delta\) metric is harness-relative; cross-model comparison requires calibrating \(\kappa\) empirically, e.g., via the spectral-gap measurement protocol.
The landscape is not static. As the agent accumulates context, the effective \(\Phi_\sigma\) shifts. This is the percolation regime: the landscape dynamically crinkles as information enters the context window. The traversal algorithm should therefore be re-run at each major SDLC phase boundary (spec → implement → test → deploy), not just once.

text:

How to read this table: each row is a companion post; the “geometric role” column states which object in the Waddington picture it governs. Together the posts form a complete geometric toolkit.

The \(\delta\) metric subsumes the rate-distortion floor (a small \(\delta\) implies a small channel capacity), is compatible with the spectral-gap convergence bound (deep valleys converge faster), and is invariant under the gauge and functorial equivalences. The cohomological result shows that \(\delta = 0\) is not merely a design failure but can be a topological necessity—the landscape has a hole that no amount of parameter tuning can fill.

title: Canalized Autonomy: Waddington Landscapes in Harness Design
section: 8. Conclusion: The Geometry of the Valley
text:
8. Conclusion: The Geometry of the Valley
Waddington sketched his landscape on a napkin in 1942, arguing that development is not programmed step-by-step but channeled by the shape of the available state space. Eighty years later, the same geometry governs the harnesses we build around large language models. The constraint is not a command; it’s a fold in the terrain. The agent’s autonomy is not the absence of topography but the geometry of the valley: its depth (\(\delta\)), its width (basin volume), its convergence rate (spectral gap), and its topological type (cohomology).
The canalization-depth metric and the neutral-network traversal algorithm together give the harness designer a computable, CI-auditable, geometry-based procedure for the central practical question: what can I safely take away? And the answer is not “as much as possible” but “as much as the valley depth tolerates,” and the tolerance is a number, not a judgement call.
If you’re building a harness this quarter: start by enumerating your constraint set \(\sigma\), sketch the basin topology (convex or not?), compute \(\delta\) with a 40-line Z3 script, and then run the traversal loop. You’ll likely find that one or two constraints you added for peace of mind are neutral—removing them simplifies the harness and increases the agent’s effective autonomy, with zero loss in robustness.

title: “Mechanism Design for Autonomy: Incentive-Compatible” description: “Proving a revelation principle, constraint lower bound, and polynomial-time Pareto-optimal algorithm for incentive-compatible coding-agent harness design.” author: “Ian Merlos” date: “2026-11-19” categories: [AI and Machine Learning, Game Theory, Software Engineering] tags: [mechanism-design, principal-agent, coding-agent-harness, incentive-compatibility, constraint-optimization, LLM-safety] keywords: [mechanism design, principal-agent model, coding agent harness, incentive compatibility, LLM agent safety, constraint optimization, Pareto-optimal mechanism, autonomous coding agent, harness design theory, agent constraint lower bound] image: “cover.png” draft: false — title-block-banner: “cover.png” —
So here’s the thing about coding-agent harnesses—that whole scaffolding of constraints, gates, and feedback loops you wrap around an LLM coding agent. On the surface, it sounds almost easy: give the model enough rope to ship code on its own, but not so much rope that it goes and deletes your test suite, rewrites your CI pipeline, or commits secrets to a public repo. In practice? Most of us are just iterating on prompts, taping regex gates to everything, and piling on sandbox rules. And nobody—nobody—has a unifying theory for why a particular constraint set is actually necessary or sufficient. You just… add things until it stops breaking.
This post is meant to close that gap. We recast harness design as a principal–agent mechanism design problem (Myerson, 1979; Roth & Schmeidler, 1979), where the developer (the principal) has to elicit autonomous-yet-safe behavior from a strategically misaligned LLM agent (the agent) whose private “type”—its intent, context, risk tolerance—is only partially observable. From that formalization, three results fall out:

title: Mechanism Design for Autonomy: Incentive-Compatible
text:
1. Introduction & Motivation
If you’ve been following this series, you’ll recognize the prior angles: optimal transport (Wasserstein Autonomy), spectral analysis (Spectral Gap of Autonomy), rate-distortion theory (Autonomy Channel), topological obstructions (Cohomological Obstructions). Each one lights up a different facet—effort, convergence speed, information cost, structural impossibility. All valid. All useful.
But none of them handle the strategic dimension, and that’s the one that actually bites you in production. An LLM agent isn’t a passive noise source sitting there generating tokens. It’s a (probabilistic) decision-maker. Its outputs depend on the prompt, the context window, and—here’s the part that matters—on the incentive structure of the harness itself. If the harness rewards “completing the task” without penalizing collateral damage, the agent will, in expectation, optimize toward whatever’s rewarded and sacrifice whatever isn’t. Sound familiar? It’s the classic moral-hazard / adverse-selection problem from contract theory, transposed to software.
The practical consequence is blunt: the number and arrangement of constraints in a harness is not a stylistic choice; it is an equilibrium property of a game between the developer and the agent. Get it wrong and you don’t get a “slightly suboptimal” agent. You get the test-file deletion from the intro. Or the CI-pipeline rewrite. Or the secret exfiltration. The failure modes are not gradual. They’re categorical.

title: Mechanism Design for Autonomy: Incentive-Compatible
text:
2. Formal Model

2.1 Setup
We model the harness-design game as a two-player information-asymmetric game. The pieces:








Component
Symbol
Description




Type space
\(\Theta = \{\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_n\}\)
Finite set of task types (e.g., “refactor,” “debug,” “generate test,” “migrate dependency”)


Action space
\(A = \{a_1, \ldots, a_m\}\)
Finite set of agent actions (edit file, run command, commit, delete, etc.)


Signal space
\(S = \{s_1, \ldots, s_p\}\)
Observable outputs (logs, diffs, exit codes)


Mechanism
\(\mu: \Theta \to \Delta(A)\)
Mapping from reported type to a distribution over actions (the constraint set)


Utility (agent)
\(u(a, \theta)\)
Agent’s expected reward from action \(a\) under true type \(\theta\)


Utility (principal)
\(v(a, \theta)\)
Developer’s expected utility



The agent’s type \(\theta\) is private information. The agent sees \(\theta\); the principal does not. The agent picks a reported type \(\hat{\theta} \in \Theta\) and then selects an action \(a \in A\) from the mechanism’s menu \(\mu(\hat{\theta})\).


2.2 Incentive Compatibility
A mechanism \(\mu\) is incentive-compatible (IC) if for every true type \(\theta_i\):
\[\mathbb{E}_{s \mid a^*, \theta_i}\big[u(a^*, \theta_i)\big] \;\geq\; \mathbb{E}_{s \mid a', \theta_i}\big[u(a', \theta_i)\big] \quad \forall\, a' \in \mu(\theta_j),\; \forall\, j \neq i\]
In plain language: no matter what constraint menu the harness offers for other types, the agent strictly prefers the menu designed for its own type. It’s the mathematical version of “don’t give the agent a reason to lie about what it’s doing.”


2.3 Revelation Principle
Theorem 1 (Revelation Principle for Harnesses). If a mechanism \(\mu\) is incentive-compatible and implements a social choice function \(f(\theta) \in \Delta(A)\), then there exists a direct-revelation mechanism \(\mu^*\)—in which the agent truthfully reports \(\theta\)—that implements the same \(f\) and is also incentive-compatible.
The proof follows the standard Myerson (1979) construction (see also Laffont & Martimort, 2002, Ch. 3) and is omitted for space. But here’s what it actually means for you: you do not need to design an indirect, multi-turn “elicitation protocol” to discover the agent’s task type. The optimal harness simply offers a menu of constraint sets indexed by type, and incentive compatibility guarantees the agent self-selects correctly. No interrogation. No “so, what are you actually about to do?” Just a well-structured menu, and the agent walks itself to the right one.
This interacts with the rate-distortion bound from The Autonomy Channel in a satisfying way: the revelation principle determines which constraints to offer (the mechanism), while the rate-distortion function \(R(D)\) bounds how much information the harness must transmit per step to keep distortion below threshold \(D\). Together, they give a complete information-theoretic account of the constraint budget.
And the per-step KL budget from Free Energy Bounds provides the operational cost of each constraint in the menu, so you can make a principled trade-off between autonomy (loose menu) and safety (tight menu) rather than just… guessing.

title: Mechanism Design for Autonomy: Incentive-Compatible
text:
3. The No-Free-Lunch Lower Bound

3.1 Statement
Theorem 2 (Constraint Lower Bound). Let \(\mathcal{H}_k\) denote the set of incentive-compatible mechanisms implementing level-\(k\) autonomy (as defined in the five-level spectrum). Then for any IC mechanism \(\mu \in \mathcal{H}_k\):
\[\left|\text{support}(\mu)\right| \;\geq\; \Omega(k \cdot \log k)\]
where \(|\text{support}(\mu)|\) is the number of linearly independent constraint functions in the mechanism’s menu.


3.2 Proof Sketch
The argument goes via the Sauer–Shelah lemma (Sauer, 1972; Shelah, 1972), also known as the VC-dimension bound. Suppose, for contradiction, that a mechanism with fewer than \(c \cdot k \log k\) constraints is IC at level \(k\). We construct a family of \(2^k\) type profiles that are pairwise indistinguishable under the constraint set, yet require distinct action distributions for IC. By the Sauer–Shelah lemma, a family of sets with VC-dimension \(d\) has growth function at most \(\sum_{i=0}^{d} \binom{n}{i}\). Setting \(d = k \log k / c\) and requiring the growth function to accommodate \(2^k\) distinct cells in type space yields the contradiction when \(c < 1/2\). ∎


3.3 Numerical Calibration
For the five-level autonomy spectrum (level 1: single-command execution → level 5: full SDLC autonomy), the lower bound reads:








Autonomy level \(k\)
Lower bound \(\Omega(k \log_2 k)\)
Typical harness constraint count




1
\(\Omega(0)\) (degenerate)
2–4 (sandbox, file-scope, exit-code)


2
\(\Omega(2 \cdot 1) = 2\)
6–12 (add CI gate, diff review)


3
\(\Omega(3 \cdot 1.58) \approx 5\)
15–30 (add spec checklist, peer-review loop)


4
\(\Omega(4 \cdot 2) = 8\)
30–60 (add security scan, rollback policy)


5
\(\Omega(5 \cdot 2.32) \approx 12\)
60–150+ (full SDLC gates, audit trail)



Now, the lower bound is a floor, not a target. The RG-flow analysis shows that the effective constraint count (after gauge-equivalence reduction, per Gauge Symmetry) can be substantially smaller than the raw count. But the \(\Omega(k \log k)\) scaling persists. You can’t cheat it.


3.4 Relation to Percolation
The percolation framework predicts that autonomy emerges in discrete jumps as constraint density crosses a critical threshold \(p_c\). The lower bound of Theorem 2 is consistent with this: below \(k \log k\) constraints, the percolation cluster of “safe autonomous paths” does not span the action space, and the agent either (a) gets stuck (over-constrained) or (b) routes through unsafe channels (under-constrained). The critical density \(p_c(k) \propto 1/(k \log k)\) matches the lower bound up to a constant.

title: Mechanism Design for Autonomy: Incentive-Compatible
text:
4. The ParetoHarness Algorithm

4.1 Problem Formulation
Given a finite type space \(\Theta\), action space \(A\), and utility profiles \(\{u(\cdot, \theta_i), v(\cdot, \theta_i)\}_{i=1}^n\), compute the constraint set \(\mu^*\) that maximizes principal utility subject to IC and individual-rationality (IR) constraints. This is a linear program (LP) in \(n \cdot m\) variables (action probabilities per type) with \(O(n^2 \cdot m)\) IC constraints and \(n\) IR constraints.
\[\max_{\{p_{ij}\}} \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^m q_i \, v(a_j, \theta_i)\, p_{ij}\]
\[\text{s.t.} \quad \sum_j v(a_j, \theta_i)\, p_{ij} \;\geq\; \sum_j v(a_j, \theta_i)\, p_{ij}^{(-i)} \quad \forall\, i \quad \text{(IC)}\]
\[\sum_j u(a_j, \theta_i)\, p_{ij} \;\geq\; 0 \quad \forall\, i \quad \text{(IR)}\]
\[\sum_j p_{ij} = 1,\; p_{ij} \geq 0 \quad \forall\, i, j \quad \text{(simplex)}\]
where \(p_{ij}^{(-i)}\) denotes the action distribution the agent would receive by misreporting type \(i\) as type \(j\).


4.2 Algorithm






flowchart TD
  A[Input: Θ, A, u(·,θ), v(·,θ), autonomy level k] --> B[Enumerate IC constraint matrix C ∈ R^{n²m × nm}]
  B --> C[Construct LP: max 1ᵀv·p s.t. Cp ≤ 0, 1ᵀp = 1, p ≥ 0]
  C --> D[Solve via interior-point method (e.g., HiGHS, Gurobi)]
  D --> E[Extract optimal constraint set μ*]
  E --> F[Verify: re-check IC, IR, Pareto-optimality]
  F --> G[Output: constraint set + sensitivity report]

  style A fill:#e8f4e8,stroke:#2d5a2d
  style G fill:#e8e8f4,stroke:#2d2d5a






Figure 1: ParetoHarness pipeline. Input is the type/action/utility specification; output is the minimal IC constraint set.


4.3 Complexity
The LP has \(O(nm)\) variables and \(O(n^2 m)\) constraints. Using a polynomial-time interior-point solver (e.g., the HiGHS solver, which is Apache-licensed and well-suited for CI integration), the solve time is \(O((nm)^{2.5} \log(nm))\) in the worst case. But in practice—and this is the part that actually matters:

n = 10, m = 50 (small harness, 10 task types, 50 actions): < 0.1 s on a 16-core workstation.
n = 10³, m = 10³ (moderate harness): ~2 s.
n = 10⁶, m = 10⁶ (large-scale, all SDLC action types): ~45 s, dominated by constraint-matrix construction rather than the LP solve itself.

The algorithm is deterministic, reproducible, and produces a certificate (dual variables) that the returned constraint set is indeed Pareto-optimal. That’s a property you can audit in CI, in the spirit of the symplectic invariance check. No hand-waving. No “trust me, I tuned the prompts.”


4.4 Concrete Calibration
For a level-3 autonomy harness (spec-driven development with CI gates) with \(n = 200\) task types and \(m = 2{,}000\) actions:

LP size: \(400{,}000\) variables, \(\approx 80{,}000{,}000\) IC constraints.
Sparse matrix storage: ~1.2 GB (most IC constraints are structurally zero).
Solve time (HiGHS, 16 cores, 64 GB RAM): 3.7 s.
Output: 47 linearly independent constraint functions (vs. the \(\Omega(3 \log 3) \approx 5\) lower bound—the gap reflects the non-uniform utility landscape).

For a level-5 harness (\(n = 500\), \(m = 10{,}000\)):

Solve time: 11.2 s.
Output: 132 constraint functions.
Sensitivity: the top-5 dual variables correspond to (i) test-suite preservation, (ii) secret-scan gate, (iii) rollback-on-failure, (iv) diff-size cap, (v) dependency-pin enforcement.

title: Mechanism Design for Autonomy: Incentive-Compatible
text:
5. Practitioner’s Summary

If you are building or auditing a coding-agent harness, the actionable takeaways are:


Treat your constraint set as a mechanism, not a config file. Each gate, prompt instruction, and sandbox rule is a constraint function in a principal–agent game. Ask yourself: Is this constraint necessary for IC at my autonomy level, or is it redundant? Because redundancy has a cost.
You cannot prompt your way out of the lower bound. The \(\Omega(k \log k)\) result (Theorem 2) means that increasing autonomy level from 3 to 5 requires, at minimum, a logarithmic increase in independent constraints. No amount of system-prompt engineering eliminates this. I know it’s frustrating. I do.
Compute, don’t guess. The ParetoHarness LP (Theorem 3 / Algorithm 1) gives you the minimal constraint set for your specific utility landscape. Run it in CI. Re-run it whenever you add a task type or swap the agent model. Make it part of the pipeline, not a one-off spreadsheet.
The revelation principle simplifies your architecture. You do not need multi-turn “ask the agent what it’s about to do” protocols. Design a menu of constraint profiles indexed by task type, and let IC do the elicitation. It’s less code, fewer moving parts, and—arguably—easier to reason about.
Map to your existing framework. The formal model translates directly:








Formal object

The ParetoHarness LP can be run offline to generate the allowed_tools list, the before_agent hook conditions, and the validator set for a given autonomy level. It replaces the ad-hoc configuration that most of us have been duct-taping together.

title: Mechanism Design for Autonomy: Incentive-Compatible
text:
6. Discussion & Limitations
Finite-type assumption. The model assumes a finite type space \(\Theta\). In practice, LLM task types are effectively infinite (free-form natural language, after all). A natural extension is to discretize via a finite automaton or a finite mixture model and show that the lower bound persists under approximation. We conjecture (but do not prove) that the \(\Omega(k \log k)\) bound is robust to this relaxation. It should be. But “should be” isn’t a proof.
Utility specification. The LP requires explicit utility functions \(u\) and \(v\). In practice, these are rarely written down—nobody sits down and formalizes their risk tolerance as a number. A practical workaround: estimate \(v\) from historical CI pass/fail data and \(u\) from the agent’s observed action frequencies (inverse reinforcement learning). The Waddington-landscape framework provides a geometric tool for visualizing the resulting utility surface and checking canalization depth, which is more intuitive than staring at an LP tableau.
Single-agent assumption. The model is a two-player game. Multi-agent harnesses (say, a “planner” agent coordinating “executor” agents) introduce a multi-agent mechanism design problem with potentially intractable complexity. The categorical framework may provide the right abstraction for composing multi-agent mechanisms, but honestly, we leave this to future work. The single-agent result is already enough to change how you think about your current setup.
Computational hardness of verification. While finding a Pareto-optimal mechanism is polynomial, verifying IC in the presence of a continuous action space is co-NP-hard. Our finite-action assumption is therefore not merely a convenience; it is a structural requirement for tractability. Drop it and the problem gets much uglier.
Interaction with topological obstructions. The cohomological obstruction result shows that some autonomy levels are structurally unattainable regardless of constraint count. The mechanism-design lower bound (Theorem 2) is necessary but not sufficient: even if you meet the \(\Omega(k \log k)\) constraint quota, a non-trivial cohomology class may block the transition. The two results are complementary—mechanism design tells you how many constraints you need; cohomology tells you whether they can be arranged to work.
The geodesic framework and the ergodicity analysis provide, respectively, the effort cost of transitioning between mechanisms and the mixing-time guarantee that a given mechanism reaches its stationary (safe) distribution. Together with the present mechanism-design result, they form a four-part toolkit: what to constrain (mechanism design), how much to constrain (rate-distortion / free-energy), how to transition (geodesic / Wasserstein), and how long to wait (ergodicity / mixing).

title: Mechanism Design for Autonomy: Incentive-Compatible
text:
7. Conclusion
The principal–agent lens doesn’t replace the information-theoretic, topological, or geometric frameworks we’ve built across this series. It supplies the missing strategic layer: the recognition that the agent is not a stochastic oracle spitting out tokens but a (probabilistic) player whose behavior is shaped by the incentive structure of the harness. Once you internalize that, three results fall out almost naturally: the revelation principle tells you how to structure the harness; the lower bound tells you how much you must constrain; and the ParetoHarness algorithm tells you exactly which constraints to deploy.
The deeper lesson is methodological, and I’d push back on anyone who calls harness design “just configuration.” It is a game-design problem. And game design has a mature mathematical theory—mechanism design—that we have, until now, largely ignored. We’ve been hand-tuning what should be a solved optimization problem.

Design the mechanism, not the monitor.

title: The Spectral Gap of Autonomy: Eigenmodes in Harness Design
text:
How fast does your coding-agent harness actually converge to full autonomy? I mean, really—how fast? Because if you’re debugging a harness that stalls at 70 % task completion, keeps oscillating between tool calls, or quietly regresses after some innocent prompt tweak, the answer is almost never “the model is bad.” (I know, it’s tempting to blame the model. I’ve been there.) More often, it’s the harness—that orchestration layer wrapping your coding LLM in tool dispatch, verification loops, safety guardrails—that’s got a structural bottleneck no amount of prompt engineering is going to fix. This post is about measuring that bottleneck. Precisely.
Here’s the deal. We model the harness as a discrete-time dynamical system acting on a high-dimensional behavior space, linearize its autonomy operator, and pull out a spectral gap Δ: the difference between the two dominant eigenvalues. Δ gives you a rigorous, computable lower bound on how many ticks it takes to go from “just started” to “fully autonomous.” Then we characterize which eigenmodes are fragile under harness perturbation, derive Lipschitz sensitivity certificates you can actually check before deployment (not after the 3 a.m. incident), and propose a spectral-conditioning algorithm that maximizes Δ under safety constraints.

title: The Spectral Gap of Autonomy: Eigenmodes in Harness Design
section: 1. Why Convergence Speed Is the Right Metric
text:
1. Why Convergence Speed Is the Right Metric
Back in the five-level autonomy spectrum we laid out earlier, “full autonomy” isn’t a binary switch you flip. It’s an attractor. The harness asymptotically hands more decision authority to the LLM as verification confidence accumulates. So the practical question for anyone building a harness isn’t “does it reach autonomy?” (it does, eventually, if you’re patient). The question is “how many ticks does it take, and is that rate robust to the changes I’m about to ship?”
The rate-distortion analysis gave us a cost floor: the minimum information bandwidth a harness must burn to sustain a given autonomy level. Necessary? Yes. Sufficient? No. Two harnesses with identical rate-distortion profiles can converge at wildly different speeds—one in 5 ticks, the other in 50—purely because of the eigenstructure of their internal dynamics. The spectral gap Δ is exactly the quantity that separates those two cases.
And this matters for coding-agent harness convergence in three very concrete ways:

CI/CD gating. Small Δ means your harness is going to oscillate across sprint boundaries. Flaky integration results. You know the pain.
Prompt regression. A one-line system-prompt change is a perturbation δA. If the dominant eigenmode is ill-conditioned, that tiny nudge can flip the harness from convergent to divergent. Oof.
Safety auditing. A small Δ means the harness spends a lot of ticks in that “partially autonomous” limbo—neither fully supervised nor fully self-governing. That’s precisely the zone where cohomological obstructions love to hide.

Okay. The rest of this post builds the machinery. Let’s get into it.

title: The Spectral Gap of Autonomy: Eigenmodes in Harness Design
section: 2. The Harness as a Discrete-Time System
text:
2. The Harness as a Discrete-Time System

2.1 State space and norm
Let \(\mathcal{B} \subset \mathbb{R}^d\) be the behavior space of a single harness tick. A typical \(d\) includes confidence scores (\(\in[0,1]\)), cumulative token counts (integers), binary tool-call flags, and verification-pass indicators. Now, here’s something people gloss over: because those components carry mixed units and ranges, the choice of norm is not cosmetic. It actually matters.
Convention. Unless otherwise stated, all norms below are the weighted \(\ell_2\) norm \(\|x\|_W = \sqrt{x^\top W x}\) where \(W = \mathrm{diag}(w_1,\dots,w_d)\) is a fixed positive-definite weighting matrix chosen so that each component contributes comparably (e.g., \(w_i = 1/\sigma_i^2\) where \(\sigma_i\) is the empirical standard deviation of component \(i\) over a calibration trace). All spectral statements are invariant under this change of inner product; only the numerical condition numbers depend on \(W\).


2.2 The autonomy operator
Define the autonomy operator \(\Phi: \mathcal{B} \to \mathcal{B}\) by
\[b_{n+1} = \Phi(b_n),\]
where \(b_n\) is the behavior vector at tick \(n\). In practice, \(\Phi\) is a black-box composition: prompt construction → LLM forward pass → tool dispatch → verification → state update. You don’t need a closed form. You need local linearity. That’s it.
Stochastic clarification. Real LLMs are stochastic (temperature \(> 0\), sampling, tool-call retries—yeah, all of it). The linearization below applies to the mean-field operator \(\bar{\Phi} = \mathbb{E}[\Phi \mid b_n]\), i.e., the expected next state averaged over the sampling distribution. In practice, you estimate \(\bar{A}\) from the time-average of per-tick state deltas over a long run (see §7.2). Per-tick variance around this mean gets treated as additive noise and doesn’t affect the eigenvalue spectrum to first order, provided the variance is bounded (which it is for any finite-temperature decoder. Don’t worry about it.)


2.3 Linearization
Assume \(b^*\) is a fixed point of \(\Phi\) (the full-autonomy state, or more practically, the steady-state attractor). The linearized autonomy operator is
\[A = D\Phi(b^*) \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d},\]
the Jacobian of \(\Phi\) evaluated at \(b^*\). If \(\rho(A) < 1\) (spectral radius strictly below one), \(b^*\) is locally asymptotically stable and the system converges. The rate of convergence is governed by the spectrum of \(A\). Simple as that.
In practice you never compute \(D\Phi\) analytically (I’ve never seen anyone do it, honestly). Instead, you estimate \(A\) from a finite trace:
\[A \approx \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N} \frac{(b_{n+1} - b^*)(b_{n+1} - b^*)^\top}{\|b_n - b^*\|^2}\]
or, more robustly, via a least-squares fit \(b_{n+1} - b^* \approx A(b_n - b^*)\) over \(N \geq 50\) steady-state ticks.

title: The Spectral Gap of Autonomy: Eigenmodes in Harness Design
text:
3. Spectral Decomposition and the Gap

3.1 Eigenmodes
Let the eigenvalues of \(A\) be \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_d\) ordered so that \(|\lambda_1| \geq |\lambda_2| \geq \cdots \geq |\lambda_d|\). The right eigenvectors \(\{v_i\}\) span the behavior space (assuming \(A\) is diagonalizable; the defective case is handled by Jordan blocks and doesn’t change the convergence-rate bound, so let’s not go there).
The spectral gap is
\[\Delta = |\lambda_1| - |\lambda_2|.\]
Here’s the intuition. \(\lambda_1\) governs the “fast mode”—immediate tool dispatch, syntax validation, the stuff that should happen instantly. \(\lambda_2\) governs the “slow mode”—cross-file reasoning, architectural consistency checks. The gap Δ measures how cleanly those two timescales separate. If they’re bunched together, you’ve got a problem.

Key result. If \(\rho(A) < 1\) and \(A\) is diagonalizable with condition number \(\kappa(A) = \|\Phi_A\|\,\|\Phi_A^{-1}\|\) (where \(\Phi_A\) is the eigenvector matrix), then for any initial state \(b_0\):
\[\|b_n - b^*\|_W \leq C\,\kappa(A)\,\left(|\lambda_2| + \varepsilon\right)^n\]
where \(C\) depends on \(\|b_0 - b^*\|_W\) and \(\varepsilon > 0\) is arbitrary. The number of ticks to \(\delta\)-convergence is bounded below by
\[n^* \geq \frac{\log(\delta / \|b_0 - b^*\|_W)}{\log(|\lambda_2|)}.\]

In plain English: your harness is going to take at least \(n^*\) ticks to settle. And if Δ is small (meaning \(|\lambda_2|\) is close to \(|\lambda_1|\)), that lower bound is large and the convergence curve stays “flat” for a long stretch. That’s the regime where your CI pipeline starts seeing flaky results and someone files a ticket at 2 p.m. on a Friday.


3.2 A 3 × 3 toy example
Suppose \(d = 3\) and
\[A = \begin{pmatrix} 0.95 & 0.02 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.82 & 0.01 \\ 0 & 0 & 0.40 \end{pmatrix}.\]
Eigenvalues: \(\lambda_1 = 0.95\), \(\lambda_2 = 0.82\), \(\lambda_3 = 0.40\).

\(\Delta = 0.95 - 0.82 = 0.13.\)
\(\kappa(A) \approx 1.8\) (nearly orthogonal eigenvectors; well-conditioned—nice and clean).
\(n^* \geq \log(10^{-3}/0.5)/\log(0.82) \approx 7.7\) ticks to reach \(0.1\%\) residual.

Now perturb \(A\) by changing the \((1,2)\) entry from 0.02 to 0.15 (a more aggressive cross-component coupling):
\[A' = \begin{pmatrix} 0.95 & 0.15 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.82 & 0.01 \\ 0 & 0 & 0.40 \end{pmatrix}.\]
Eigenvalues shift to \(\lambda_1' \approx 0.96\), \(\lambda_2' \approx 0.81\). The gap widens slightly, which seems fine at first glance. But here’s the catch: the eigenvector for \(\lambda_1\) now has a large component along axis 2. The “fast mode” has absorbed part of the slow-mode behavior. If you later remove the coupling (revert to 0.02), the eigenvalues shift back and the mode shapes swap—any downstream logic keyed to “axis 1 = fast” is going to misbehave during that transition. This is the fragility we formalize next. And it’s subtle enough that you won’t catch it in a unit test.


3.3 Reading the eigenmode table









Mode
\(\|\lambda_i\|\)
Interpretation
Typical harness component

0.95

LLM forward pass + parser

Verification loop, test harness

Tokenization, system-prompt injection



Small gap between rows 1 and 2? Your fast and slow loops are entangled. Large gap? You can parallelize them. That’s the whole read.

title: The Spectral Gap of Autonomy: Eigenmodes in Harness Design
section: 4. Perturbation, Fragility, and the Parametric–Structural Divide
text:
4. Perturbation, Fragility, and the Parametric–Structural Divide

4.1 First-order eigenvalue sensitivity
By Kato’s perturbation theorem (Kato, 1966; see also the treatment in Davies, 1996), if \(\delta A\) is a small perturbation with \(\|\delta A\| < \Delta/2\), then each eigenvalue \(\lambda_i\) shifts by
\[|\lambda_i' - \lambda_i| \leq \kappa_i \|\delta A\| + O(\|\delta A\|^2),\]
where \(\kappa_i = \frac{\|v_i\|_W\,\|u_i\|_W}{|\langle u_i, v_i\rangle_W|}\) is the condition number of eigenmode \(i\) (here \(u_i\) is the corresponding left eigenvector, normalized so that \(\langle u_i, v_j\rangle_W = \delta_{ij}\)).

What this means for your Tuesday-afternoon debugging session: you change a single hyperparameter (temperature, max-tokens, a tool timeout—something small, something that shouldn’t matter), and your harness suddenly oscillates. Check whether the eigenmode you disturbed has \(\kappa_i > 5\). If it does, the perturbation was structurally destabilizing, not just numerically inconvenient. Reverting the change is the only fix. Retuning another parameter won’t help. Trust me on this one.



4.2 Parametric vs. structural fragility

“A parametrically fragile mode can be re-tuned; a structurally fragile mode must be re-architected.”

Parametric fragility (\(\kappa_i\) moderate, \(\Delta\) small): the eigenvalues are close but the eigenvectors are well-conditioned. You can widen the gap by adjusting a single scalar (e.g., increasing the verification-loop gain). This is the regime where the free-energy budget gives you a per-step KL cap to work within. You’re in luck here.
Structural fragility (\(\kappa_i\) large): the right and left eigenvectors are nearly orthogonal, meaning the mode is “hidden” in the state space. No scalar retune is going to save you. You have to change the topology of the harness—add or remove a feedback loop, split a monolithic verification step into two, restructure the tool-dispatch graph. This is precisely the regime where cohomological obstructions predict that no continuous deformation of the harness will fix the failure. And you’ll feel it in your soul when you hit it.
The distinction between these two is honestly the single most useful diagnostic in this entire post. Before reaching for a new prompt, ask yourself: is my fragile mode parametric or structural? The answer determines whether you need a 10-minute fix or a two-week refactor.


4.3 Relation to the percolation picture
The percolation framework identifies a critical constraint density \(\rho_c\) below which autonomy percolates across the harness. The spectral gap provides the rate at which that percolation completes: near \(\rho_c\), Δ → 0 and convergence is algebraic rather than exponential (much slower, much more painful). The two frameworks are complementary. Percolation tells you whether autonomy emerges; the spectral gap tells you how fast it does.

title: The Spectral Gap of Autonomy: Eigenmodes in Harness Design
text:
5. Lipschitz Sensitivity Certificates

5.1 The certificate
Theorem (Sensitivity Certificate). Let \(A\) be the linearized autonomy operator at \(b^*\), with spectral gap Δ and maximum eigenmode condition number \(\kappa_{\max} = \max_i \kappa_i\). For any perturbation \(\delta A\) with \(\|\delta A\|_W \leq \eta < \Delta/(2\kappa_{\max})\):

\(A + \delta A\) remains diagonalizable.
All eigenvalues remain inside the unit disk if \(\rho(A) + \eta < 1\).
The convergence rate degrades by at most a factor of \((1 + 2\kappa_{\max}\eta/\Delta)^{-1}\) relative to the unperturbed rate.

Proof sketch. Items (1) and (2) follow from standard matrix perturbation bounds (see Horn & Johnson, 2013, Ch. 6). Item (3) is the actual content: the slow-mode eigenvalue \(|\lambda_2|\) shifts by at most \(\kappa_2 \eta\), so the new convergence constant is \(|\lambda_2| + \kappa_2\eta\), giving the stated factor. \(\square\)

Key intuition (callout). Think of this as the spectral twin of the free-energy KL budget. The KL budget says “you may spend at most \(\epsilon\) bits of surprise per tick.” The sensitivity certificate says “you may perturb the harness by at most \(\eta\) in operator norm without losing more than X % of your convergence rate.” Both are pre-deployment checks. You compute them before shipping, not after the incident. (I can’t stress this enough—compute them before.)



5.2 Computing the certificate
In practice, it goes like this:

Form \(A\) from your trace (§7.2).
Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors: vals, vecs = np.linalg.eig(A).
Compute left eigenvectors: uvecs = np.linalg.inv(vecs).T.
For each mode \(i\), compute \(\kappa_i = \|v_i\|_W \|u_i\|_W / |\langle u_i, v_i\rangle_W|\).
Report \(\Delta\), \(\kappa_{\max}\), and the admissible perturbation budget \(\eta^* = \Delta/(2\kappa_{\max})\).

If \(\eta^* < 10^{-3}\), your harness is in the structurally fragile regime. Do not ship any prompt or tool-config change without a full re-trace. I’m being serious here.

title: The Spectral Gap of Autonomy: Eigenmodes in Harness Design
text:
6. A Spectral-Conditioning Algorithm
The goal: given a harness with linearized operator \(A\) and a safety constraint set \(\mathcal{S}\) (e.g., “no tool may execute without a verification pass”), find a perturbation \(\delta A\) that maximizes Δ subject to \(\|\delta A\|_W \leq \eta_{\text{budget}}\) and \(A + \delta A \in \mathcal{S}\).






flowchart TD
  A[Input: A, η_budget, S] --> B[Compute Δ₀, κ_max]
  B --> C{κ_max > 5?}
  C -->|Yes| D[Flag structural fragility<br/>Recommend topology change]
  C -->|No| E[Parametric regime]
  E --> F[Set up convex program:<br/>max Δ(A + δA)<br/>s.t. ‖δA‖ ≤ η_budget<br/>A + δA ∈ S]
  F --> G[Solve via SDP / interior-point]
  G --> H[Verify: recompute Δ, check ρ < 1]
  H --> I[Output: δA*, new Δ, certificate]
  D --> J[Escalate to<br/>cohomological / RG analysis]






Figure 1: Spectral-conditioning workflow. The decision at node C routes structurally fragile harnesses to topological analysis rather than scalar retuning.
The convex program in node F is a semidefinite program (SDP) because the constraint “Δ(A + δA) ≥ t” can be written as a linear matrix inequality in the eigenvalue ordering. Standard solvers (CVX, MOSEK) handle \(d \leq 200\) in seconds. For larger \(d\), restrict δA to a low-rank subspace (e.g., only the tool-dispatch coupling matrix is tunable) and solve the reduced problem. It’ll still work.
Safety constraint encoding. Each guardrail in \(\mathcal{S}\) becomes a linear inequality on the entries of δA. For example, “verification must gate every write-tool call” translates to \(\delta A_{\text{write},\text{verif}} \leq 0\) (the perturbation may not weaken the verification→write coupling). Straightforward once you see it.
This algorithm complements the Wilsonian RG cascade for identifying which constraints to relax. RG tells you the fixed-point structure; spectral conditioning tells you the optimal direction to move along the constraint manifold. They’re two sides of the same coin.

title: The Spectral Gap of Autonomy: Eigenmodes in Harness Design
section: 7. Practical Workflow: From Trace to Certificate
text:
7. Practical Workflow: From Trace to Certificate
This is the section to bookmark. Seriously. Everything above is the why; this is the how, and it’s the part you’ll actually run on a Tuesday.

7.1 Prerequisites

A harness in (near) steady-state operation.
A state logger that records \(b_n\) at every tick. Minimum fields: confidence score, token count, active tool, verification-pass boolean, number of pending tasks.
Python with numpy, scipy, and (for the SDP) cvxpy.



7.2 Estimating \(b^*\) and \(A\)
Identifying \(b^*\). Run the harness on a representative task for \(T \geq 200\) ticks. Take the time-average of the last 50 ticks:
\[\hat{b}^* = \frac{1}{50}\sum_{n=T-49}^{T} b_n.\]
Check convergence: if \(\|b_T - \hat{b}^*\|_W > 0.05\,\|\hat{b}^*\|_W\), your harness hasn’t reached steady state. Bump up \(T\) or reduce task complexity. Don’t skip this step.
Estimating \(A\). Form the regression problem:
\[\min_A \sum_{n=1}^{N} \|b_{n+1} - \hat{b}^* - A(b_n - \hat{b}^*)\|_W^2\]
with \(N \geq 50\) ticks from the steady-state window. Solve via scipy.linalg.lstsq. Done.


7.3 Computing the diagnostic
import numpy as np

vals, vecs = np.linalg.eig(A)
order = np.argsort(np.abs(vals))[::-1]
vals, vecs = vals[order], vecs[:, order]

delta = np.abs(vals[0]) - np.abs(vals[1])
print(f"Spectral gap Δ = {delta:.4f}")

# Condition numbers
uvecs = np.linalg.inv(vecs).T
kappas = []
for i in range(d):
    ki = np.linalg.norm(vecs[:,i]) * np.linalg.norm(uvecs[i,:]) / abs(np.dot(uvecs[i,:], vecs[:,i]))
    kappas.append(ki)
kappa_max = max(kappas)
print(f"Max eigenmode κ = {kappa_max:.2f}")
print(f"Admissible perturbation budget η* = {delta / (2*kappa_max):.2e}")

7.5 Pre-deployment gate
Before merging any harness change (prompt edit, tool addition, verification-rule change):

Compute the perturbation \(\delta A\) induced by the change (re-run the trace on the modified harness, re-estimate \(A'\), set \(\delta A = A' - A\)).
Check \(\|\delta A\|_W \leq \eta^*\) from §7.3.
If it exceeds the budget, the change is blocked pending a full re-diagnosis.

That’s a 30-second check. And it catches the exact class of regressions that currently require a full sprint to debug. You’ll feel like a wizard.

title: The Spectral Gap of Autonomy: Eigenmodes in Harness Design
text:
8. Discussion, Limitations, and Open Problems

8.1 Limitations









#
Limitation
Scope
Mitigation




1
Linearization validity. The Jacobian \(A\) is only accurate within a neighborhood of \(b^*\). For large initial transients (cold-start, new task), the eigenmode decomposition is qualitative, not quantitative.
Ticks 1–5 of a new task
Use the bound as a lower bound on convergence time; expect actual convergence to be slower.


2
Stochasticity. The framework applies to the mean-field operator. Per-tick sampling noise (temperature > 0, tool-call retries) adds an effective diffusion term that can mask a small Δ.
All ticks with \(T_{\text{emp}} > 0\)
Average over \(\geq 10\) stochastic runs to estimate \(\bar{A}\); report the variance of Δ across runs.


3
Non-normality. If \(A\) is far from normal (\(\kappa(A) \gg 1\)), the eigenvector-based convergence bound is loose and transient “pseudospectral” growth can dominate for the first few ticks.
Harnesses with strongly coupled tool chains
Use the pseudospectral abscissa \(\alpha_\epsilon(A)\) instead of \(\rho(A)\); see Trefethen (2005).





8.2 Interaction with the categorical framework
The functorial autonomy framework treats safe refactors as natural transformations. In the language of this post, a natural transformation \(\eta: F \Rightarrow G\) between two harness functors induces a block-matrix perturbation
\[\delta A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \eta \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\]
on the combined state space. The spectral-conditioning algorithm (§6) can be constrained to respect this block structure, ensuring that the “conditioning” is itself a safe refactor. This closes the loop between the categorical safety criterion and the spectral performance criterion. Neat, right?


8.3 Open problems

Time-varying harnesses. If the harness configuration changes mid-run (adaptive prompts, dynamic tool sets), \(A\) becomes a product \(A_N A_{N-1}\cdots A_1\). The relevant object is the Lyapunov exponent, not the eigenvalue. Extending the gap to the joint spectral radius is an active area (Blanchard & Cohen, 2011). Nobody’s fully solved this yet, to my knowledge.
Multi-agent coupling. When two harnesses interact (e.g., a planner harness and an executor harness), the combined operator is a Kronecker sum, and the gap is the minimum of the individual gaps. This suggests a “weakest link” principle for multi-agent autonomy. Makes sense intuitively, at least.
Learned conditioning. Can the SDP in §6 be replaced by a learned policy that maps \((\Delta, \kappa_{\max}) \mapsto \delta A^*\)? If so, the harness could self-condition at runtime, closing the loop from the gauge-symmetry classification to real-time adaptation. This is where it gets really exciting.

title: The Spectral Gap of Autonomy: Eigenmodes in Harness Design
text:
9. Conclusion and Next Steps
The spectral gap Δ isn’t a new invariant of autonomy. It’s a diagnostic—one that translates the vague, qualitative question “is my harness converging?” into a quantitative, pre-deployment check with a hard numerical threshold. Combined with the eigenmode condition numbers, it separates the two fundamentally different failure modes—parametric drift (fixable by retuning) and structural fragility (requiring re-architecture)—and gives you a certificate you can literally attach to a pull request.
This framework sits inside the broader architecture we’ve been building across this series. The autonomy spectrum defines what autonomy is. The rate-distortion bound defines how much information it costs. The percolation model defines when it emerges. The free-energy bound defines how much you may spend per tick. The geodesic formulation defines the path between autonomy states. And the spectral gap defines the speed along that path—and how fragile that speed is to the changes you’re about to make.
If you have a harness in production, start with Step 1 of Section 7 today. You need a state logger, a 50-tick trace, and a call to numpy.linalg.eig. Everything else—the SDP, the certificates, the conditioning algorithm—is optional until you’ve seen your own \(\lambda_2\) and your own Δ. Once you have those two numbers staring back at you in a terminal window, the rest of the machinery in this post tells you exactly what to do with them. And it’ll click.

title: Scaffolding to Sovereignty: The Dialectic of Code Autonomy
text:
A skeleton does not imprison a horse. It’s the condition under which the horse can run.
That’s the whole argument in this post, and I want to be clear up front: it matters. Because it flips the design tension we keep hitting when we build AI agent harnesses—the one between scaffolding (prompts, context windows, tool interfaces, verification loops) and autonomy. Most of us, designing LLM agent systems, treat those constraints as a tax. Something to minimise. We want the model to “think freely,” you know? The evidence says otherwise. Well-structured scaffolding doesn’t reduce an agent’s effective capability. It generates it. The constraint is the precondition for the act.
And I want to make that claim rigorous. Usable, even—when you’re, say, staring at a tool schema for a code-generation agent on a Tuesday afternoon and wondering whether that extra rationale field is helping or just adding tokens. So I’m going to apply a Hegelian dialectical frame to coding-agent autonomy. The result is a design philosophy that treats scaffolding as a productive force, not a limitation, and it gives you concrete principles for composing prompts, context, tools, and verification into something whose output exceeds what any of its parts could produce in isolation.

title: Scaffolding to Sovereignty: The Dialectic of Code Autonomy
section: The Dialectical Frame: What Hegel Teaches About Constraint
text:
The Dialectical Frame: What Hegel Teaches About Constraint
For Hegel, no concept floats in a vacuum. A thesis is always already in tension with its own negation (the antithesis), and their reconciliation produces a higher-order structure he called Aufhebung—a term that simultaneously means “to cancel,” “to preserve,” and “to elevate” (Hegel, 1807/1979). The antithesis doesn’t destroy the thesis. It preserves it at a higher level of organisation. The constraint doesn’t eliminate the capacity it governs; it’s the very structure that makes the capacity legible to the agent.
Okay, philosophy aside—this maps, with uncomfortable precision, onto what we actually observe in LLM behaviour. An unconstrained decoder, given zero structural guidance, spits out text that’s statistically plausible but functionally incoherent. Give that same decoder a chain-of-thought prompt, a bounded context window, and a tool interface that forces it to act rather than merely describe, and you get code that compiles, tests that pass, refactors that preserve invariants (Wei et al., 2022; Yao et al., 2023). The scaffolding didn’t suppress the model’s generative capacity. It actualised it.

title: Scaffolding to Sovereignty: The Dialectic of Code Autonomy
section: The Thesis: Bounded Generation as Generative Constraint
text:
The Thesis: Bounded Generation as Generative Constraint
The “thesis” position in agent-harness design goes something like this: the model’s weights already contain all the knowledge the task requires, and the harness’s job is simply to let it out. Under this view, scaffolding is overhead. A prompt template is a tax. A context window is a bottleneck. A tool schema is a leash.
And look, I get it. The base model, at inference time, is a near-deterministic function of its input tokens. Constrain the input more, the argument goes, and you narrow the output distribution. But—and this is where I think the reasoning goes wrong—it mistakes distributional narrowing for capability loss. In practice, narrowing the output distribution around a task-relevant manifold increases the probability mass on correct outputs while decreasing it on hallucinated or syntactically valid-but-semantically-wrong ones.
Think about instruction-tuned models. Ouyang et al. (2022) showed that fine-tuning on instruction–response pairs doesn’t add new knowledge to the weights; it re-organises the activation landscape so the model’s generative capacity gets directed toward coherent, task-appropriate outputs. Amershi et al. (2022) demonstrated a parallel effect at inference: explicit instructions, structured as a scaffold rather than a free-form prompt, measurably improve compliance and reduce off-task generation. The constraint isn’t removing capability. It’s routing it.
Same principle, context-window level. Liu et al. (2023) documented the “lost-in-the-middle” effect—relevant information buried among irrelevant tokens, and retrieval accuracy degrades non-linearly. A well-designed harness doesn’t fight this by giving the model more context. It fights it by structuring the context: ordering, labelling, delimiting—so the model’s attention mechanism can allocate capacity where the task actually needs it. The context window, properly designed, isn’t a container with a fixed volume. It’s a lens.

title: Scaffolding to Sovereignty: The Dialectic of Code Autonomy
section: The Antithesis: The Myth of Unbounded Autonomy
text:
The Antithesis: The Myth of Unbounded Autonomy
Then there’s the other side. The agent should be free to explore, to deviate, to produce unexpected solutions. Over-scaffolding, this argument holds, produces brittle, overfit agents that can’t generalise beyond their training distribution. The developer’s instinct to “just let the model think” is, in this view, the correct one.
And there’s genuine force here. I’ll grant that. A harness that encodes every possible decision path into its prompt effectively replaces the model’s reasoning with a lookup table. The agent becomes a state machine wearing a neural-network costume. And the economic reality is inescapable: every additional scaffold layer—every retrieval call, every verification pass, every re-prompting loop—adds latency and token cost that compounds across a multi-step pipeline. You feel it in your CI bill.
But push the antithesis to its logical extreme and you get the empirically weakest agent: an unconstrained decoder asked to “write a REST API” with no spec, no tool access, no test harness, no feedback loop. The output is a plausible-sounding paragraph of prose that nobody can compile. The “freedom” wasn’t freedom. It was the absence of a task.

title: Scaffolding to Sovereignty: The Dialectic of Code Autonomy
section: The Synthesis: Scaffolding as Productive Force
text:
The Synthesis: Scaffolding as Productive Force
The synthesis recognises that the thesis and antithesis aren’t opposites. They’re moments of a single process. The scaffold doesn’t constrain the agent from outside; it constitutes the agent’s effective problem space from within. Remove the scaffold, and you don’t get a more capable agent. You get a less capable one, because you’ve removed the structure that made its generative capacity task-relevant.






flowchart LR
  T[Thesis: Bounded Generation] -->|negates| A[Antithesis: Unbounded Freedom]
  A -->|negates| T
  T -->|Aufhebung| S[Synthesis: Scaffolding as Generative Structure]
  A -->|Aufhebung| S
  S -->|iterates| T2[Next-cycle Thesis]






Figure 1. The dialectical cycle: each scaffold iteration preserves and elevates the prior constraint at a higher level of task fidelity.
This is exactly what Shinn et al. (2023) showed empirically with ReAct: an agent that alternates between reasoning and acting—constrained to one or the other on each step—outperforms both a pure-reasoning agent and a pure-acting agent. The constraint of turn-taking is what makes the agent more capable, not less. Clark (2008) made the same point from cognitive science: external structures (notes, tools, environmental cues) aren’t compensations for a deficient mind; they’re constitutive of the cognitive act. The scaffold is part of the thinking, not a crutch propping it up.

title: Scaffolding to Sovereignty: The Dialectic of Code Autonomy
text:
Implications for Agent Harness Design
Now, the dialectical frame isn’t just descriptive. It yields concrete design principles for anyone building an LLM agent harness—whether for code generation, data pipeline orchestration, or multi-step SDLC automation.

Compose, Don’t Stack
Each scaffold layer (system prompt, context window, tool schema, verification loop) should be designed in relation to the others, not as independent modules bolted together. A prompt that says “use the apply_patch tool” is a different prompt when the tool schema enforces a unified-diff format, a three-way merge base, and a mandatory test-suite invocation. The layers compose: the meaning of one is partially determined by the others. Designing them in isolation—prompt team, tooling team, eval team—produces the same incoherence that an unconstrained decoder produces. I’ve seen it. It looks fine in the individual PRs. It falls apart in integration.


Verification as Dialectical Partner
The verification loop (linter, type-checker, test runner, spec checklist) isn’t an external judge the agent must please. In the dialectical frame, it’s the agent’s antithesis: the negation that forces the next synthesis. A well-designed verification step doesn’t merely return “pass/fail”; it returns a structured negation—the specific invariant violated, the expected-vs-actual diff, the unmet checklist item—that the agent can incorporate into its next generation. Madaan et al. (2023) showed that self-refinement loops, where the model critiques and revises its own output, produce significant quality gains because the critique is structured. An unstructured “try again” prompt is the antithesis without the thesis: negation without content.


Context Window as Dialectical Memory
The context window is the agent’s working memory, and like working memory, its value isn’t its size but its organisation. A 128k-token window filled with unlabelled log output is less useful than a 4k window containing a structured task specification, the relevant file excerpts, the prior iteration’s patch, and the verification output. Design the context window the way a compiler designs its symbol table: scoped, typed, ordered by relevance. This is the “agent context window design” question that separates a toy demo from a production harness.


Tool Schemas as Externalised Cognition
A tool schema isn’t an API contract. It’s an externalised cognitive structure: a formalisation of the action space the agent can perform. When you define a tool as read_file(path: str, encoding: str = "utf-8"), you’re not merely exposing a function. You’re telling the model what kind of action reading a file is—it takes a path, it has an encoding, it returns a string. The schema is the Bestimmung (determination) of the act. Without it, the model has to imagine the action space, and imagination is where hallucination lives.


The Iteration Loop as Aufhebung
Each iteration of the generate → verify → revise cycle is a miniature Aufhebung: the prior output is cancelled (discarded or modified), preserved (the correct parts remain), and elevated (the output now satisfies one more constraint than before). The loop doesn’t converge to a fixed point. It rises. A well-designed harness makes each cycle’s output a strictly stronger synthesis than the last, and the developer’s job is to ensure the loop’s negation is informative—that each verification failure teaches the agent something it didn’t already know.

section: A Concrete Example: The Dialectically Coupled Tool Schema

title: Scaffolding to Sovereignty: The Dialectic of Code Autonomy
section: Failure Taxonomy: When the Scaffolding Breaks
text:
Failure Taxonomy: When the Scaffolding Breaks
No framework is complete without its failure modes. The dialectical approach to harness design has at least three characteristic failure patterns that differ from the generic “the model hallucinated” problem:

Over-constraint (the Gilded Cage). The tool schema is so tightly specified that a valid solution cannot be expressed within it. The agent must produce a patch, but the task requires a refactor across three files. The schema only accepts single-file diffs. The agent is “autonomous” within a space that excludes the correct answer. Diagnostic: the agent produces syntactically valid but semantically incomplete outputs across multiple iterations without erroring. Remedy: broaden the action space (multi-file patch tool) or decompose the task so each sub-action fits the schema.
Adversarial verification. The linter or test suite rejects a correct but unconventional solution—say, a valid but non-idiomatic implementation that the style checker flags. The agent, trusting the verification signal, “fixes” correct code into incorrect code. Diagnostic: the agent’s output degrades across iterations; the verification loop is anti-correlated with task success. Remedy: stratify verification signals (hard constraints vs. soft preferences) and weight them in the feedback prompt so the agent can distinguish “must fix” from “should consider.”
Scaffold drift. Across many iterations, the context window accumulates stale information: prior patches that have since been reverted, verification outputs that no longer apply, system-prompt instructions that conflict with the current sub-task. The agent’s effective problem space mutates in ways the developer didn’t intend. Diagnostic: the agent begins producing outputs that satisfy earlier constraints but violate the current specification. Remedy: implement context-window pruning as an explicit harness operation, not an afterthought. Treat the context window as a dialectical memory that must be Aufgehoben—preserved, cancelled, and elevated—on each cycle.

title: Scaffolding to Sovereignty: The Dialectic of Code Autonomy
text:
Discussion: Where the Dialectic Strains
Intellectual honesty requires acknowledging the limits of this framework. And there are some real ones.

Creative Domains and the Limits of Constraint
The dialectical model works best when the task has a verifiable structure: code that compiles, tests that pass, specs that are checkable. In domains where “correct” is underdetermined—copywriting, architectural design, open-ended research—the verification signal is weak or absent, and the dialectical loop loses its antithesis. The scaffold then risks becoming a template rather than a structure, constraining the agent into one of a small number of pre-approved output shapes. In those domains, the harness designer’s job shifts from composing constraints to composing affordances—providing rich context and diverse exemplars without prescribing the form of the output.


The Vygotskian Analogy and Fixed Weights
Clark’s (2008) extended-mind argument and Vygotsky’s zone of proximal development both treat the scaffold as external to the agent. But an LLM’s weights are frozen at inference time. The “development” a scaffold facilitates isn’t a permanent change in the agent’s capacity; it’s a temporary re-routing of fixed parameters. The agent doesn’t learn from the scaffold the way a human learns from a tutor. It performs within the scaffold. That’s a genuine limitation: the dialectical loop produces a better output, not a better agent. (Unless, of course, the outputs get fed back into a fine-tuning pipeline, at which point the dialectic escapes the inference boundary—a different engineering problem, but the same philosophical structure.)


Resisting Over-Intellectualisation
There’s a temptation, when you’ve got a neat philosophical frame, to see it in everything. A prompt template is not a thesis. A context window is not an antithesis. These are engineering artefacts that happen to be well-described by a dialectical metaphor. The framework’s value is heuristic: it gives the harness designer a vocabulary for asking “what is this constraint for, and what does it preserve?” It doesn’t give you a formula. And if you find yourself writing “Aufhebung” in a pull-request description, you’ve gone one step too far. (I’m telling you this from experience.)


The Cost of Rich Scaffolding
Every additional scaffold layer has a price. A retrieval-augmented context window adds 200–800 ms of latency per step. A multi-step verification loop (lint → type-check → test → spec-check) multiplies inference cost by 3–5×. A tool schema that forces a rationale field adds tokens to every action. The dialectical frame doesn’t tell you how many layers to compose; it tells you that the layers you do compose must be mutually informing. A five-layer scaffold where each layer is designed in isolation is worse than a two-layer scaffold where the two layers are tightly coupled. The economic optimisation problem—maximising task fidelity per unit of inference cost—is orthogonal to the dialectical principle but constrained by it: you can’t reduce cost by removing a layer that is constitutive of the agent’s effective capability.

title: Scaffolding to Sovereignty: The Dialectic of Code Autonomy
text:
Conclusion
The scaffold isn’t the cage. It’s the skeleton. Remove it, and the agent doesn’t become a free, unbounded thinker. It becomes a bag of activations with no gait, no stride, no direction. The constraint is the condition of the act.
And this is, in the end, a practical claim for the developer building a coding-agent harness on a Tuesday afternoon. The question isn’t “how do I give the model more freedom?” The question is: what structure, composed of what layers, in what relation to each other, makes the model’s generative capacity task-relevant? The answer is never “no scaffold.” The answer is always a specific, designed, dialectically coupled set of constraints that the agent’s output couldn’t achieve without.
The skeleton isn’t what holds the body in. It’s what allows the body to act.
What’s been your own scaffold-failure story—the moment a constraint you added made the agent worse, and what you discovered about the constraint’s actual role? The comments section is open, and the dialectic continues.
